q: What are the four fundamental freedoms that Canadian law protects?
opts: Conscience and religion; thought and expression; peaceful assembly; association
Speech and press; bearing arms; free movement; access to healthcare
Religion, education, movement, and employment rights
Press, religion, privacy, and the right to vote
exp: Canadian law protects freedom of conscience and religion; freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression (including freedom of speech and of the press); freedom of peaceful assembly; and freedom of association. These date back 800 years to the Magna Carta of 1215.

q: What is habeas corpus?
opts: The right to vote in federal elections
The right to challenge unlawful detention by the state
The right to a fair and speedy trial
The right to address Parliament directly
exp: Habeas corpus, which comes from English common law, is the right to challenge unlawful detention by the state.

q: What does the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms protect?
opts: Only the rights of citizens born in Canada
Only criminal rights during court proceedings
Mobility, Aboriginal, official language rights, and multiculturalism among others
Only the rights of permanent residents and refugees
exp: The Charter, which became part of Canada's Constitution in 1982, protects mobility rights, Aboriginal peoples' rights, official language rights, minority language educational rights, and multiculturalism among other fundamental rights.

q: What are mobility rights under the Canadian Charter?
opts: The right to travel abroad using only a Canadian passport
The right to live, work, enter, and leave Canada freely and apply for a passport
The right to relocate to any country in the world
The right to use public transit anywhere in Canada
exp: Mobility rights mean Canadians can live and work anywhere they choose in Canada, enter and leave the country freely, and apply for a passport.

q: What are three responsibilities of Canadian citizenship?
opts: Loyalty to Canada, recycling newspapers, and serving in the navy
Learning both official languages, voting in all elections, joining a union
Obeying the law, caring for one's family, and serving on a jury
Buying Canadian products, owning a business, and conserving water
exp: Three key responsibilities of citizenship are: obeying the law, taking responsibility for oneself and one's family, and serving on a jury when called to do so.

q: What is the meaning of the Remembrance Day poppy?
opts: To honour our Sovereign and the Royal Family
To celebrate Confederation and Canada's founding
To remember the sacrifice of Canadians who served or died in wars
To honour Prime Ministers who have passed away
exp: The red poppy is worn on Remembrance Day (November 11) to remember the sacrifice of Canadians who have served or died in wars up to the present day.

q: What does the equality of women and men mean in Canada?
opts: Women and men must have equal seats in Parliament
Men and women are equal under the law
Women and men must earn identical salaries by law
Women and men must serve equal time in the military
exp: In Canada, men and women are equal under the law. Canada's openness and generosity do not extend to practices that tolerate spousal abuse, honour killings, female genital mutilation, forced marriage or other gender-based violence.

q: What does voting in elections mean as a Canadian responsibility?
opts: Canadians are legally required to vote or face a fine
The right to vote carries a responsibility to vote in federal, provincial, and local elections
Only citizens born in Canada are required to vote
Voting is optional and carries no civic responsibility
exp: Voting in elections is described in the guide as both a right and a responsibility. The right to vote comes with a responsibility to vote in federal, provincial or territorial and local elections.

q: What does 'helping others in the community' mean as a Canadian responsibility?
opts: Paying a mandatory community tax each year
Donating at least ten percent of your income to registered charities
Working for a government agency for at least one year
Volunteering time freely to help people and gain skills and contacts
exp: Helping others in the community means volunteering — millions of Canadians freely donate their time to help people in need, assist at schools, volunteer at food banks or charities, or encourage newcomers to integrate. Volunteering is an excellent way to gain useful skills and develop friends and contacts.

q: What does 'protecting and enjoying our heritage and environment' mean as a Canadian responsibility?
opts: Joining an environmental or heritage political party
Every citizen helps avoid waste and protects Canada's natural and cultural heritage for future generations
Only paying the taxes that fund national parks and museums
Purchasing only Canadian-made goods and products
exp: Every citizen has a role to play in avoiding waste and pollution while protecting Canada's natural, cultural and architectural heritage for future generations.

q: What does serving on a jury mean as a Canadian responsibility?
opts: All Canadians must serve in the military reserves
Jury duty is a fully voluntary community service program
Only licensed lawyers and legal professionals may serve on juries
When called, you are legally required to serve — it upholds an impartial justice system
exp: When called to serve on a jury, you are legally required to do so. Serving on a jury is a privilege that makes the justice system work as it depends on impartial juries made up of citizens.

q: What is multiculturalism described as in the Canadian Charter?
opts: A law requiring all Canadians to speak a second language
A fundamental characteristic of Canadian heritage where Canadians celebrate diversity and respect pluralism
A policy that only applies to recent immigrants
A temporary government program first introduced in 2000
exp: The Charter describes multiculturalism as a fundamental characteristic of the Canadian heritage and identity. Canadians celebrate the gift of one another's presence and work hard to respect pluralism and live in harmony.

q: What does Aboriginal peoples' rights under the Charter mean?
opts: The Charter replaces all Aboriginal treaty rights entirely
Charter rights will not adversely affect any Aboriginal treaty or other rights
Aboriginal peoples are fully exempt from Canadian laws
Aboriginal peoples have no distinct rights under the Charter
exp: Under the Charter, Aboriginal peoples' rights means the rights guaranteed in the Charter will not adversely affect any treaty or other rights or freedoms of Aboriginal peoples.

q: What does official language rights mean under the Charter?
opts: All Canadians must speak both English and French fluently
French and English have equal status in Parliament and throughout the government
French language rights are protected only in Quebec
English is the sole official language of federal courts
exp: Official Language Rights and Minority Language Educational Rights means French and English have equal status in Parliament and throughout the government. The federal government is required by law to provide services throughout Canada in English and French.

q: What is the rule of law in Canada?
opts: Only the Prime Minister is above the law
The law can be changed by the Prime Minister at any time
Laws apply only to ordinary citizens and not the government
Individuals and governments are regulated by law — no person is above it
exp: One of Canada's founding principles is the rule of law. Individuals and governments are regulated by laws and not by arbitrary actions. No person or group is above the law.

q: Is there compulsory military service in Canada?
opts: Yes, all citizens must serve at least two years in the military
No, there is no compulsory military service in Canada
Yes, but only for men between the ages of 18 and 25
Yes, but only during a wartime declared by Parliament
exp: There is no compulsory military service in Canada. However, serving in the regular Canadian Forces (navy, army and air force) is described as a noble way to contribute to Canada and an excellent career choice.

q: What does obeying the law mean as a Canadian responsibility?
opts: Only following federal laws, not provincial ones
Obeying laws is optional for permanent residents
One of Canada's founding principles — no one is above the law
Only obeying the laws you personally agree with
exp: Obeying the law is one of Canada's founding principles — the rule of law. Individuals and governments are regulated by laws and not by arbitrary actions, and no person or group is above the law.

q: What does 'taking responsibility for oneself and one's family' mean as a Canadian value?
opts: The government provides for all citizens' basic daily needs
Family responsibility only applies to parents with children under age 12
This value only applies to immigrants, not to natural-born citizens
Getting a job, caring for one's family, and working hard are important Canadian values
exp: Getting a job, taking care of one's family and working hard in keeping with one's abilities are important Canadian values. Work contributes to personal dignity and self-respect, and to Canada's prosperity.

q: What are the two official languages of Canada?
opts: English and Spanish
English and French
French and Inuktitut
English and Mandarin
exp: English and French are the two official languages of Canada and are important symbols of identity. English speakers (Anglophones) and French speakers (Francophones) have lived together in partnership for more than 300 years.

q: What does Canada's diversity include regarding gay and lesbian Canadians?
opts: Gay and lesbian Canadians have limited legal rights in some provinces
Gay and lesbian Canadians enjoy full legal protection and equal treatment, including civil marriage
Same-sex relationships are only recognized in certain provinces
Gay and lesbian rights are not yet addressed in Canadian law
exp: Canada's diversity includes gay and lesbian Canadians, who enjoy the full protection of and equal treatment under the law, including access to civil marriage.

q: Who are the three founding peoples of Canada?
opts: French, English, and Irish
Aboriginal, French and British
Inuit, French and American
First Nations, Métis and European
exp: To understand what it means to be Canadian, it is important to know about the three founding peoples — Aboriginal, French and British.

q: Where are the ancestors of Aboriginal peoples believed to have come from?
opts: Europe
Africa
Asia
South America
exp: The ancestors of Aboriginal peoples are believed to have migrated from Asia many thousands of years ago. They were well established here long before explorers from Europe first came to North America.

q: What are the three distinct groups that the term 'Aboriginal peoples' refers to today?
opts: Cree, Inuit, and Algonquin
Indian (First Nations), Inuit, and Métis
Mohawk, Inuit, and Huron
First Nations, Acadian, and Inuit
exp: Today, the term Aboriginal peoples refers to three distinct groups: Indian (First Nations), Inuit, and Métis. About 65% of Aboriginal people are First Nations, while 30% are Métis and 4% are Inuit.

q: What does the word 'Inuit' mean?
opts: The hunters
The people
The northerners
The Arctic dwellers
exp: The Inuit, which means 'the people' in the Inuktitut language, live in small, scattered communities across the Arctic. Their knowledge of the land, sea and wildlife enabled them to adapt to one of the harshest environments on earth.

q: Who are the Métis?
opts: A distinct people of mixed Aboriginal and European ancestry who speak their own dialect, Michif
Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Coast and Rocky Mountains
French settlers who first came to Canada in the 1600s
Inuit peoples who relocated from the Arctic to the Prairies
exp: The Métis are a distinct people of mixed Aboriginal and European ancestry, the majority of whom live in the Prairie provinces. They come from both French- and English-speaking backgrounds and speak their own dialect, Michif.

q: From 1800s to 1980s, what did the federal government do with many Aboriginal children?
opts: Sent them to study in France or Britain for education
Gave them special rights and designated reserve lands
Placed them in residential schools to educate and assimilate them into mainstream Canadian culture
Encouraged them to move to urban centres for work
exp: From the 1800s until the 1980s, the federal government placed many Aboriginal children in residential schools to educate and assimilate them into mainstream Canadian culture. The schools were poorly funded and inflicted hardship on the students; some were physically abused. Aboriginal languages and cultural practices were mostly prohibited. In 2008, Ottawa formally apologized to the former students.

q: When did Ottawa formally apologize to former residential school students?
exp: In 2008, Ottawa formally apologized to the former students of residential schools.

q: How many Anglophones (English speakers) and Francophones (French speakers) are there in Canada?
opts: 20 million Anglophones and 10 million Francophones
18 million Anglophones and 7 million Francophones
15 million Anglophones and 15 million Francophones
25 million Anglophones and 5 million Francophones
exp: Today, there are 18 million Anglophones — people who speak English as a first language — and seven million Francophones — people who speak French as their first language.

q: Which is the only officially bilingual province in Canada?
opts: Quebec
Ontario
New Brunswick
Prince Edward Island
exp: New Brunswick is the only officially bilingual province. While the majority of Francophones live in Quebec, one million Francophones live in Ontario, New Brunswick and Manitoba, with a smaller presence in other provinces.

q: Who are the Acadians?
opts: English settlers who arrived in Atlantic Canada in the 1700s
Descendants of French colonists settling the Maritimes in 1604, many deported in the Great Upheaval
Métis peoples who originally settled along the New Brunswick coast
Inuit communities that established villages throughout Nova Scotia
exp: The Acadians are descendants of French colonists who began settling in what are now the Maritime provinces in 1604. Between 1755 and 1763, during the war between Britain and France, more than two-thirds of the Acadians were deported from their homeland — an event known as the Great Upheaval. Despite this ordeal, the Acadians survived and maintained their unique identity.

q: Who are the Quebecers?
opts: The people of Quebec, mostly French-speaking descendants of 8,500 French settlers
Only those who were born in Quebec City
All people who currently reside in the city of Quebec
French Canadians who live outside of Quebec province
exp: Quebecers are the people of Quebec, the vast majority French-speaking. Most are descendants of 8,500 French settlers from the 1600s and 1700s and maintain a unique identity, culture and language. The House of Commons recognized in 2006 that the Quebecois form a nation within a united Canada.

q: What did the House of Commons recognize about the Quebecois in 2006?
opts: That Quebec should become a fully independent country
That the Quebecois form a nation within a united Canada
That French is the only official language within Quebec
That Quebec holds the right to separate from Canada
exp: The House of Commons recognized in 2006 that the Quebecois form a nation within a united Canada.

q: What percentage of Aboriginal people are First Nations, Métis, and Inuit respectively?
opts: 50% First Nations, 40% Métis, 10% Inuit
About 65% First Nations, 30% Métis, 4% Inuit
70% First Nations, 20% Métis, 10% Inuit
80% First Nations, 15% Métis, 5% Inuit
exp: About 65% of the Aboriginal people are First Nations, while 30% are Métis and 4% are Inuit.

q: Canada is known around the world as what kind of country?
opts: A republic governed by an elected president
A country governed entirely by a council of premiers
A strong and free country — the only constitutional monarchy in North America
A country with no official religion, culture, or heritage
exp: Canada is known around the world as a strong and free country. We are the only constitutional monarchy in North America. Our institutions uphold a commitment to Peace, Order and Good Government.

q: What is the largest religious affiliation in Canada?
opts: Protestant
Muslim
Catholic
Jewish
exp: The great majority of Canadians identify as Christians. The largest religious affiliation is Catholic, followed by various Protestant churches. The numbers of Muslims, Jews, Hindus, Sikhs and members of other religions are also growing.

q: Who was the first European to draw a map of Canada's East Coast?
opts: Jacques Cartier
Samuel de Champlain
John Cabot
Henry Hudson
exp: European exploration began in earnest in 1497 with the expedition of John Cabot, who was the first to draw a map of Canada's East Coast. He set foot on Newfoundland or Cape Breton Island and claimed the New Founde Land for England.

q: Who claimed Canada for France and what word gave Canada its name?
opts: John Cabot; the word 'new land' in Latin
Jacques Cartier; the Iroquoian word 'kanata' meaning village
Samuel de Champlain; the French word for 'great river'
Henry Hudson; the Dutch word for 'northern land'
exp: Between 1534 and 1542, Jacques Cartier made three voyages across the Atlantic, claiming the land for King Francis I of France. Cartier heard two captured guides speak the Iroquoian word kanata, meaning 'village.' By the 1550s, the name of Canada began appearing on maps.

q: Who founded Quebec City and when?
opts: Jacques Cartier in 1534
Samuel de Champlain in 1608
John Cabot in 1497
Pierre de Monts in 1604
exp: In 1608 Champlain built a fortress at what is now Quebec City. In 1604, the first European settlement north of Florida was established by French explorers Pierre de Monts and Samuel de Champlain, first on St. Croix Island, then at Port-Royal in Acadia.

q: What was the Battle of the Plains of Abraham and when did it occur?
opts: A 1759 British victory near Quebec City — both commanders Wolfe and Montcalm were killed
A French victory over Britain in 1713 fought near Montreal
A 1775 border battle between Canada and the United States
An Indigenous victory over British forces fought in 1763
exp: In 1759, the British defeated the French in the Battle of the Plains of Abraham at Quebec City — marking the end of France's empire in America. The commanders of both armies, Brigadier James Wolfe and the Marquis de Montcalm, were killed leading their troops in battle.

q: What did the Quebec Act of 1774 do?
opts: It made Quebec an independent country from Britain
It banned the French language from all Quebec public life
It allowed religious freedom for Catholics and French civil law, while maintaining British criminal law
It made English the only official language of Quebec
exp: The Quebec Act of 1774 accommodated the principles of British institutions to the reality of the province. It allowed religious freedom for Catholics and permitted them to hold public office — a practice not then allowed in Britain. The Quebec Act restored French civil law while maintaining British criminal law.

q: Who were the United Empire Loyalists and how many came to Canada?
opts: French settlers loyal to France; about 10,000 came to Canada
Irish immigrants loyal to Britain; about 5,000 came to Canada
People loyal to the British Crown who fled the American Revolution; more than 40,000 came
British soldiers who remained in Canada after the War of 1812
exp: In 1776, the 13 British colonies to the south of Quebec declared independence and formed the United States. More than 40,000 people loyal to the Crown, called 'Loyalists,' fled the oppression of the American Revolution to settle in Nova Scotia and Quebec. About 3,000 black Loyalists, freedmen and slaves also came north seeking a better life.

q: What was the first representative assembly in Canada and where was it elected?
opts: The first representative assembly was elected in Halifax, Nova Scotia, in 1758
The first assembly was elected in Quebec City in 1791
The first assembly was elected in Upper Canada in 1792
The first assembly was elected in Montreal in 1800
exp: Democratic institutions developed gradually and peacefully. The first representative assembly was elected in Halifax, Nova Scotia, in 1758. Prince Edward Island followed in 1773, New Brunswick in 1785.

q: What did the Constitutional Act of 1791 do?
opts: It created Canada as a fully independent country
It gave women the right to vote for the first time
It divided Quebec into Upper and Lower Canada and granted elected legislative assemblies
It formally united Upper and Lower Canada into a single province
exp: The Constitutional Act of 1791 divided the Province of Quebec into Upper Canada (later Ontario), which was mainly Loyalist, Protestant and English-speaking, and Lower Canada (later Quebec), heavily Catholic and French-speaking. The Act also granted legislative assemblies elected by the people for the first time.

q: Who led Upper Canada toward abolishing slavery and when?
opts: Sir John A. Macdonald introduced abolition legislation in 1867
Lieutenant Governor John Graves Simcoe led Upper Canada toward abolition in 1793
Lord Durham recommended abolition in his 1838 report to Britain
Robert Baldwin achieved abolition through responsible government reforms in 1848
exp: In 1793, Upper Canada, led by Lieutenant Governor John Graves Simcoe, a Loyalist military officer, became the first province in the British Empire to move toward abolition of slavery. In 1807, the British Parliament prohibited the buying and selling of slaves, and in 1833 abolished slavery throughout the Empire.

q: What was the War of 1812?
opts: A war between Canada and France fought over fur trade routes
A war between Britain and France fought on Canadian soil
An Indigenous uprising against European settlers in the interior
A US invasion of Canada repelled by Canadian volunteers, First Nations, and British soldiers
exp: Believing it would be easy to conquer Canada, the United States launched an invasion in June 1812. Canadian volunteers and First Nations, including Shawnee led by Chief Tecumseh, supported British soldiers in Canada's defence. By 1814, the American attempt to conquer Canada had failed. The present-day Canada-U.S.A. border is partly an outcome of the War of 1812.

q: What is Confederation and when did it occur?
opts: The signing of a major trade deal with the US in 1867
The birth of Canada on July 1, 1867, when the British North America Act united four provinces
The formal union of Canada and Britain as one nation in 1867
The first Canadian election, held on July 1, 1870
exp: The British Parliament passed the British North America Act in 1867. The Dominion of Canada was officially born on July 1, 1867. The four founding provinces were Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Until 1982, July 1 was celebrated as 'Dominion Day' — today it is officially known as Canada Day.

q: Who was Canada's first Prime Minister?
opts: Sir Wilfrid Laurier
Sir George-Étienne Cartier
Sir John Alexander Macdonald
Sir Leonard Tilley
exp: In 1867, Sir John Alexander Macdonald, a Father of Confederation, became Canada's first Prime Minister. Born in Scotland on January 11, 1815, he came to Upper Canada as a child. Parliament has recognized January 11 as Sir John A. Macdonald Day. His portrait is on the $10 bill.

q: When was the Canadian Pacific Railway completed and what was its significance?
opts: 1871 — it linked Ontario and Quebec by rail for the first time
1873 — it was built primarily to transport goods to the United States
1880 — it was built specifically to bring settlers to the Prairies
November 7, 1885 — a symbol of unity connecting Canada coast to coast
exp: On November 7, 1885, a powerful symbol of unity was completed when Donald Smith (Lord Strathcona) drove the last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The project was financed by British and American investors and built by both European and Chinese labour. The CPR's 'ribbons of steel' fulfilled a national dream.

q: What was the Chinese Head Tax and when did the government apologize for it?
opts: A tax on Chinese goods imported to Canada; apologized for in 1982
A race-based entry fee charged to Chinese immigrants after the CPR; government apologized in 2006
A special business tax on Chinese-Canadian businesses; apologized for in 1988
A tax levied to fund CPR construction that was never officially apologized for
exp: After the CPR was built, Chinese workers were subject to discrimination, including the Head Tax, a race-based entry fee. The Government of Canada apologized in 2006 for this discriminatory policy.

q: Who was Sir Wilfrid Laurier?
opts: Canada's first Prime Minister, who served from 1867 to 1873
The first French-Canadian Prime Minister since Confederation, featured on the $5 bill
The Father of Confederation who represented Quebec at the 1864 conference
The first Governor General appointed after Canada achieved full independence
exp: Sir Wilfrid Laurier became the first French-Canadian prime minister since Confederation and encouraged immigration to the West. His portrait is on the $5 bill.

q: What happened at the Battle of Vimy Ridge?
opts: Canadian forces liberated the Netherlands from German occupation in 1945
Canadian and British forces together captured a key German port in 1918
Canadian forces defeated American troops along the border in 1813
In April 1917 all four Canadian divisions fought together, capturing Vimy Ridge with 10,000 casualties
exp: The Canadian Corps captured Vimy Ridge in April 1917, with 10,000 killed or wounded, securing the Canadians' reputation for valour as the 'shock troops of the British Empire.' April 9 is celebrated as Vimy Day. One Canadian officer said: 'It was Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific on parade... In those few minutes I witnessed the birth of a nation.'

q: How many Canadians served in the First World War and how many were killed?
opts: 300,000 served; 30,000 were killed in combat
More than 600,000 served; 60,000 were killed and 170,000 wounded
500,000 served; 50,000 were killed in action
200,000 served; 20,000 were killed in battle
exp: More than 600,000 Canadians served in the First World War, most of them volunteers, out of a total population of eight million. In total 60,000 Canadians were killed and 170,000 were wounded.

q: When did women gain the right to vote in federal elections in Canada?
exp: In 1917, thanks to women's leadership, the federal government of Sir Robert Borden gave women the right to vote in federal elections — first to nurses at the battle front, then to women related to men in active wartime service. In 1918, most Canadian female citizens aged 21 and over were granted the right to vote in federal elections.

q: Who was Agnes Macphail?
opts: Canada's first female Prime Minister
A farmer and teacher who became the first woman MP in 1921
The first woman appointed to the Supreme Court of Canada
The founder of the women's suffrage movement in Canada
exp: In 1921, Agnes Macphail, a farmer and teacher, became the first woman MP in Canada.

q: What happened on D-Day, June 6, 1944?
opts: Canada formally declared war on Germany at Normandy
Canadian forces liberated Paris from German occupation
Canada signed a peace treaty with Imperial Japan
15,000 Canadians stormed Juno Beach in the Allied D-Day invasion of Normandy
exp: In the epic invasion of Normandy in northern France on June 6, 1944 (D-Day), 15,000 Canadian troops stormed and captured Juno Beach from the German Army — approximately one in ten Allied soldiers on D-Day was Canadian. The Canadian Army liberated the Netherlands in 1944–45 and helped force the German surrender of May 8, 1945.

q: How many Canadians served in the Second World War and how many were killed?
opts: Approximately 500,000 served; around 30,000 were killed in action
Over one million Canadians and Newfoundlanders served; about 44,000 were killed
Approximately 750,000 served; around 60,000 were killed in combat
Approximately 250,000 served; around 10,000 were killed in action
exp: More than one million Canadians and Newfoundlanders (Newfoundland was a separate British entity at the time) served in the Second World War, out of a population of 11.5 million. Of these, 44,000 were killed.

q: What was the Royal Canadian Navy's role in the Second World War?
opts: It transported troops to Europe but did not engage in combat
It fought exclusively in the Pacific theatre against Japan
It invaded Normandy on D-Day as the lead naval force
It protected Atlantic convoys from German submarines, ending the war as the third-largest navy
exp: The Royal Canadian Navy (RCN) saw its finest hour in the Battle of the Atlantic, protecting convoys of merchant ships against German submarines. Canada's Merchant Navy helped to feed, clothe and resupply Britain. At the end of the Second World War, Canada had the third-largest navy in the world.

q: What was the responsible government system established in Canada?
opts: A system where provinces can override any federal law
A system where the Governor General manages the country day to day
If the government loses a confidence vote it must resign — first in Nova Scotia in 1847–48
A system where the Senate controls the elected government
exp: The first British North American colony to attain full responsible government was Nova Scotia in 1847–48. Responsible government means: if the government loses a confidence vote in the assembly it must resign. This is the system Canada has today.

q: When did Newfoundland and Labrador join Canada?
exp: Newfoundland and Labrador joined Canada in 1949, becoming the 10th province.

q: Who was Louis Riel and what did he lead?
opts: The first French-Canadian Prime Minister after Confederation
Canada's second Prime Minister, who oversaw the building of the CPR
A First Nations chief who negotiated the numbered treaties with Ottawa
A Métis leader who led the Red River uprising and 1885 rebellion — father of Manitoba
exp: When Canada took over the vast northwest region from the Hudson's Bay Company in 1869, the 12,000 Métis of the Red River were not consulted. Louis Riel led an armed uprising and seized Fort Garry. Canada established a new province — Manitoba. Riel led a second rebellion in 1885. He is seen by many as a hero, a defender of Métis rights and the father of Manitoba.

q: When was the North West Mounted Police established and what did it later become?
opts: Established by Prime Minister Macdonald in 1873 to pacify the West — today it is the RCMP
Established in 1867 as the Canadian Border Police, later became the RCMP
Established in 1885 after the Canadian Pacific Railway was completed
Established in 1896 during the height of the Klondike Gold Rush
exp: Prime Minister Macdonald established the North West Mounted Police (NWMP) in 1873 to pacify the West and assist in negotiations with the Indians. Today, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) or 'the Mounties' are the national police force and one of Canada's best-known symbols.

q: What was the term 'Dominion of Canada' and who suggested it?
opts: Suggested by Sir John A. Macdonald, inspired by the British word for colony
Suggested by Sir Leonard Tilley, inspired by Psalm 72 referring to 'dominion from sea to sea'
Suggested personally by Queen Victoria in a letter to Parliament
Suggested by Sir Wilfrid Laurier as a symbol of French-Canadian national pride
exp: Sir Leonard Tilley, an elected official and Father of Confederation from New Brunswick, suggested the term Dominion of Canada in 1864. He was inspired by Psalm 72 in the Bible which refers to 'dominion from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth.'

q: When was Nunavut created?
exp: Nunavut, meaning 'our land' in Inuktitut, was established in 1999 from the eastern part of the Northwest Territories. Its capital is Iqaluit and its population is about 85% Inuit.

q: What was the Klondike Gold Rush?
opts: A major gold rush in British Columbia in the 1850s
Thousands of miners rushed to the Yukon during the Gold Rush of the 1890s
A significant gold discovery in Alberta in 1947
A gold rush in northern Ontario in the early 1900s
exp: Thousands of miners came to the Yukon during the Gold Rush of the 1890s. Mining remains a significant part of the Yukon's economy today.

q: What was the Statute of Westminster?
opts: A 1982 Canadian law that patriated the constitution from Britain
A 1931 British law granting Canada and other Dominions full legislative independence
The original British North America Act that created Canada in 1867
A Quebec law establishing French as the province's sole official language
exp: After the First World War, the British Empire evolved into a free association of states known as the British Commonwealth of Nations. Canada remains a leading member of the Commonwealth to this day.

q: When did Aboriginal people gain the right to vote in federal elections?
exp: Most Canadians of Asian descent had in the past been denied the vote in federal and provincial elections. In 1948 the last of these, the Japanese-Canadians, gained the right to vote. Aboriginal people were granted the vote in 1960. Today every citizen over the age of 18 may vote.

q: What are some great Canadian discoveries and inventions?
opts: The automobile, the airplane, and the World Wide Web
Telephone, snowmobile, standard time zones, insulin, and the pacemaker
The radio, television, and the first personal computer
The steam engine, the electric light bulb, and penicillin
exp: Famous Canadian inventions and discoveries include: Alexander Graham Bell — the telephone; Joseph-Armand Bombardier — the snowmobile; Sir Sandford Fleming — the worldwide system of standard time zones; Sir Frederick Banting and Charles Best — insulin; and Dr. John A. Hopps — the first cardiac pacemaker.

q: Who discovered insulin and what is its significance?
opts: Dr. Wilder Penfield — used to treat neurological brain disorders
Sir Frederick Banting and Charles Best — discovered insulin to treat diabetes, saving millions of lives
Reginald Fessenden — used in pioneering early radio communications
Dr. John A. Hopps — invented the first cardiac pacemaker device
exp: Sir Frederick Banting of Toronto and Charles Best discovered insulin, a hormone to treat diabetes that has saved 16 million lives worldwide.

q: What sport did Canadian James Naismith invent and in what year?
opts: Football in 1880
Basketball in 1891
Ice hockey in 1875
Lacrosse in 1860
exp: Basketball was invented by Canadian James Naismith in 1891.

q: What is Terry Fox known for?
opts: He was the first Canadian to win an Olympic gold medal
He was a famous Canadian hockey player for the Maple Leafs
He was the first Canadian astronaut to go to space
In 1980 he ran the Marathon of Hope across Canada after losing his leg to cancer
exp: In 1980, Terry Fox, a British Columbian who lost his right leg to cancer at the age of 18, began a cross-country run, the 'Marathon of Hope,' to raise money for cancer research. He became a hero to Canadians. While he did not finish the run and ultimately lost his battle with cancer, his legacy continues through yearly fundraising events in his name.

q: When was oil discovered in Alberta and what did it begin?
opts: 1930 — it began Canada's mining industry
1947 — it began Canada's modern energy industry
1965 — it began Canada's export economy
1980 — it began large-scale oil sands development
exp: The discovery of oil in Alberta in 1947 began Canada's modern energy industry.

q: What is the Canada Health Act?
opts: A law requiring all Canadians to purchase private health insurance
A federal act ensuring common elements and a basic standard of healthcare coverage across Canada
A law that created the Canadian university medical school system
A Quebec law that established the provincial health insurance system
exp: The Canada Health Act ensures common elements and a basic standard of coverage for healthcare across Canada.

q: When was unemployment insurance (now called employment insurance) introduced?
exp: Unemployment insurance (now called 'employment insurance') was introduced by the federal government in 1940.

q: When were the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans established?
exp: Old Age Security was devised as early as 1927, and the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans were established in 1965.

q: What military alliance did Canada join with other democratic Western nations?
opts: The League of Nations after World War I
The Commonwealth Defence Alliance with Britain
The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and NORAD with the United States
The Pacific Security Pact with Japan and Australia
exp: Canada joined with other democratic countries of the West to form the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), a military alliance, and with the United States in the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD).

q: What was Canada's role in the Korean War (1950–53)?
opts: Canada led all United Nations forces throughout Korea
Canada participated in the UN operation defending South Korea, with 500 dead and 1,000 wounded
Canada provided only financial support and no troops
Canada did not participate in the Korean War at all
exp: Canada joined international organizations such as the United Nations. It participated in the UN operation defending South Korea in the Korean War (1950–53), with 500 dead and 1,000 wounded.

q: What was the Quiet Revolution in Quebec?
opts: A peaceful Indigenous land rights movement across Quebec
An era of rapid change in 1960s Quebec where French-Canadian culture flourished and many sought separation
A series of protests against conscription in Quebec during WWII
A movement that led directly to Quebec's official bilingualism in 1969
exp: Quebec experienced an era of rapid change in the 1960s known as the Quiet Revolution. French-Canadian society and culture flourished in the postwar years. Many Quebecers sought to separate from Canada.

q: What is the Official Languages Act and when was it passed?
opts: Passed in 1969, it guarantees French and English services across the federal government
A 1982 act that made French the only language of Quebec
A 1867 act that established English as Canada's official language
A 1971 act that established Canada's multiculturalism policy
exp: In 1963 Parliament established the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism. This led to the Official Languages Act (1969), which guarantees French and English services in the federal government across Canada.

q: What happened in the Quebec sovereignty referendum of 1980?
opts: Quebec voted to separate from the rest of Canada
The movement for Quebec sovereignty was defeated in a provincial referendum
Quebec voted to become an officially bilingual province
The referendum was cancelled because of very low voter turnout
exp: The movement for Quebec sovereignty gained strength but was defeated in a referendum in the province in 1980. Though sovereignty was again defeated in a second referendum in 1995, the autonomy of Quebec within Canada remains a lively topic.

q: When was the Canadian Space Agency established and what has it contributed?
opts: 1975 — it launched the first Canadian satellite into orbit
2000 — Canada joined the International Space Station program
1969 — a Canadian was part of the Apollo moon landing
Since 1989 — Canadian astronauts have explored space, often using the Canadian-built Canadarm
exp: Since 1989, the Canadian Space Agency and Canadian astronauts have participated in space exploration, often using the Canadian-designed and built Canadarm.

q: What did Wayne Gretzky accomplish and which team did he play for?
opts: He won five Olympic gold medals representing Team Canada
One of hockey's greatest players ever, he played for the Edmonton Oilers from 1979 to 1988
He invented the modern Canadian style of hockey in the 1970s
He was the very first Canadian player in the NHL
exp: One of the greatest hockey players of all time, Wayne Gretzky, played for the Edmonton Oilers from 1979 to 1988.

q: What did Rick Hansen do in 1985?
opts: He won multiple gold medals at the 1985 Paralympic Games
He circled the globe in a wheelchair, raising funds for spinal cord research
He became the first Canadian to successfully summit Mount Everest
He swam across the English Channel to raise money for cancer research
exp: In 1985, fellow British Columbian Rick Hansen circled the globe in a wheelchair to raise funds for spinal cord research.

q: What is La Francophonie and when did Canada help found it?
opts: A Quebec arts festival that was established in 1967
An international association of French-speaking countries that Canada helped found in 1970
A Canadian government department managing French-language services
A French-Canadian political party that was established in 1960
exp: In 1970, Canada helped found La Francophonie, an international association of French-speaking countries.

q: What is the Group of Seven in art?
opts: Seven Canadian Prime Ministers who shaped modern Canada
Seven influential French-Canadian writers of the 1960s
A group of seven Indigenous artists who pioneered Aboriginal art
Founded in 1920, a group of painters who captured Canada's rugged wilderness landscapes
exp: In the visual arts, Canada is historically perhaps best known for the Group of Seven, founded in 1920, who developed a style of painting to capture the rugged wilderness landscapes.

q: What happened to Japanese Canadians during the Second World War and when did the government apologize?
opts: They were celebrated for their wartime service; no apology was needed
They were interned only briefly in 1944; the government apologized in 1950
The state forcibly relocated them and sold their property without compensation; Canada apologized in 1988
They were relocated to Quebec for safety; the government has never formally apologized
exp: The state of war and public opinion in B.C. led to the forcible relocation of Canadians of Japanese origin by the federal government and the sale of their property without compensation. This occurred even though the military and the RCMP told Ottawa that they posed little danger to Canada. The Government of Canada apologized in 1988 for wartime wrongs and compensated the victims.

q: What are the three key facts about Canada's system of government?
opts: A republic, a democracy, and a federation
A federal state, a parliamentary democracy, and a constitutional monarchy
A monarchy, a senate system, and a federation
A democracy, a bilingual state, and a confederation
exp: There are three key facts about Canada's system of government: our country is a federal state, a parliamentary democracy, and a constitutional monarchy.

q: What are the three parts of Parliament?
opts: The President, the Senate, and the Supreme Court
The Sovereign (Queen or King), the Senate, and the House of Commons
The Prime Minister, the Cabinet, and the Senate
The Governor General, the House of Commons, and the Supreme Court
exp: Parliament has three parts: the Sovereign (Queen or King), the Senate, and the House of Commons.

q: What is Canada's head of state?
opts: The Prime Minister
The Governor General
The hereditary Sovereign (Queen or King)
The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
exp: As a constitutional monarchy, Canada's Head of State is a hereditary Sovereign (Queen or King), who reigns in accordance with the Constitution: the rule of law.

q: What is the role of the Governor General?
opts: To lead the federal government and set national policy
The Sovereign is represented by the Governor General, appointed on the advice of the Prime Minister
To serve as the presiding head of the Senate
To manage and administer federal elections on behalf of the Crown
exp: The Sovereign is represented in Canada by the Governor General, who is appointed by the Sovereign on the advice of the Prime Minister, usually for five years. In each of the ten provinces, the Sovereign is represented by the Lieutenant Governor.

q: What is the difference between the head of state and the head of government in Canada?
opts: There is no difference — they are the same person
The head of state is the Sovereign; the head of government is the Prime Minister, who directs the country
The head of state is the Governor General; the head of government is the Senate
The head of state is elected; the head of government is appointed
exp: There is a clear distinction in Canada between the head of state — the Sovereign — and the head of government — the Prime Minister, who actually directs the governing of the country.

q: How are Senators chosen and how long do they serve?
opts: Elected by Canadian citizens in provincial elections; serve four-year terms
Appointed by the Governor General on the PM's advice; serve until age 75
Appointed by provincial premiers from regional nominees; serve until age 70
Elected by Members of Parliament in a secret vote; serve six-year terms
exp: Senators are appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister and serve until age 75.

q: What are the federal government's responsibilities?
opts: Education, health, property and civil rights
Municipal government, highways, and natural resources
Defence, foreign policy, trade, currency, criminal law, and citizenship
Agriculture only — shared with the provinces
exp: The federal government takes responsibility for matters of national and international concern. These include defence, foreign policy, interprovincial trade and communications, currency, navigation, criminal law and citizenship.

q: What are the provinces responsible for?
opts: Defence, foreign policy, and criminal law
Currency, banking, and immigration policy
International trade and citizenship matters
Municipal government, education, health, natural resources, and highways
exp: The provinces are responsible for municipal government, education, health, natural resources, property and civil rights, and highways.

q: What jurisdictions do the federal government and provinces share?
opts: Criminal law and education
Agriculture and immigration
Healthcare and national defence
Banking and natural resources
exp: The federal government and the provinces share jurisdiction over agriculture and immigration.

q: What does 'confidence of the House' mean?
opts: The House of Commons must formally trust the Governor General
Cabinet ministers must retain House confidence and resign if defeated in a non-confidence vote
The Senate must approve all Cabinet ministerial appointments
The Prime Minister must be elected directly by all sitting MPs
exp: Cabinet ministers are responsible to the elected representatives, which means they must retain the 'confidence of the House' and have to resign if they are defeated in a non-confidence vote.

q: What are the three branches of Canada's government?
opts: The Crown, the Senate, and the House of Commons
The Executive, Legislative, and Judicial branches
The Federal, Provincial, and Municipal branches
The Governor General, the Prime Minister, and the Supreme Court
exp: The interplay between the three branches of government — the Executive, Legislative, and Judicial — which work together but also sometimes in creative tension, helps to secure the rights and freedoms of Canadians.

q: What does the Premier do in a province?
opts: Represents the Crown at the provincial level in official ceremonies
Leads the provincial government, similar to how the Prime Minister leads federally
Presides over the provincial legislature as its official Speaker
Appoints all provincial court judges on the premier's recommendation
exp: In each province, the Premier has a role similar to that of the Prime Minister in the federal government, just as the Lieutenant Governor has a role similar to that of the Governor General.

q: What is a bill in the Canadian legislative process?
opts: A proposal for a new law that must pass both chambers and receive royal assent
A request for funding submitted by a province to Ottawa
A formal summary of the Prime Minister's annual policy priorities
A formal complaint submitted by an MP to Parliament
exp: Both the House of Commons and the Senate consider and review bills (proposals for new laws). No bill can become law in Canada until it has been passed by both chambers and has received royal assent, granted by the Governor General on behalf of the Sovereign.

q: What role does local or municipal government play?
opts: Municipal governments have jurisdiction over criminal law and policing
Municipal governments oversee public education and provincial healthcare delivery
Municipal governments are accountable directly to the federal government
Municipal councils pass by-laws covering planning, roads, transit, and local services
exp: Local or municipal government plays an important role in the lives of citizens. Municipal governments usually have a council that passes laws called 'by-laws.' Municipalities are normally responsible for urban or regional planning, streets and roads, sanitation, snow removal, firefighting, ambulance, recreation facilities, public transit and some local health and social services.

q: What is the constitutional monarchy and what does the Crown symbolize?
opts: A system in which the monarch personally makes all laws for Canada
A purely ceremonial arrangement with no real legal or political power
A system in which the Governor General holds supreme authority over Parliament
A system where the Head of State reigns under the Constitution, representing all government authority
exp: As a constitutional monarchy, Canada's Head of State is a hereditary Sovereign who reigns in accordance with the Constitution: the rule of law. The Crown is a symbol of government, including Parliament, the legislatures, the courts, police services and the Canadian Forces.

q: How are members of Parliament chosen?
opts: They are appointed by the United Nations
They are chosen by provincial premiers directly
They are elected by voters in their local constituency (riding)
They are elected by landowners and police chiefs
exp: Canadians vote in elections for the people they want to represent them in the House of Commons. Members of the House of Commons are also known as members of Parliament or MPs. Each riding elects one MP.

q: How many electoral districts does Canada have?
exp: Canada is divided into 308 electoral districts, also known as ridings or constituencies. An electoral district is a geographical area represented by a member of Parliament (MP). The citizens in each electoral district elect one MP.

q: Who is eligible to vote in a federal election?
opts: All residents of Canada aged 18 and over
Canadian citizens at least 18 years old on voting day and on the voters' list
Canadian citizens and permanent residents aged 18 and over
Anyone who has lived in Canada for more than one year
exp: You are eligible to vote in a federal election or cast a ballot in a federal referendum if you are: a Canadian citizen; at least 18 years old on voting day; and on the voters' list.

q: When must federal elections be held?
opts: The third Monday of October every four years, though the PM may call an early election
The first Monday of October every three years, on a fixed schedule
Every five years with no fixed day required under the Constitution
Whenever the Governor General dissolves Parliament at the Senate's formal request
exp: Under legislation passed by Parliament, federal elections must be held on the third Monday in October every four years following the most recent general election. The Prime Minister may ask the Governor General to call an earlier election.

q: What is the secret ballot?
opts: A ballot mailed secretly and directly to registered voters before election day
The legally protected right to vote in private, with no one permitted to watch
A special ballot used only in Senate leadership elections
A ballot reserved exclusively for voters who require accessibility accommodations
exp: Canadian law secures the right to a secret ballot. This means that no one can watch you vote and no one should look at how you voted. No one, including family members, your employer or union representative, has the right to insist that you tell them how you voted.

q: What is a majority government?
opts: When the party in power holds at least half the seats in the House of Commons
A government where the PM's party holds more than 50% of Senate seats
A government supported by more than 75% of all Canadian voters
A government formed by two parties working in coalition
exp: Ordinarily, after an election, the leader of the political party with the most seats in the House of Commons is invited by the Governor General to form the government. If the party in power holds at least half of the seats in the House of Commons, this is called a majority government. If the party in power holds less than half of the seats, this is called a minority government.

q: What is the Official Opposition?
opts: A group of appointed senators whose role is to oppose government legislation
The largest opposition party in the House of Commons, known as Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition
A committee of independent MPs assigned to review and amend government bills
A body appointed by the Governor General to formally review Cabinet decisions
exp: The other parties that are not in power are known as opposition parties. The opposition party with the most members of the House of Commons is the Official Opposition or Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. The role of opposition parties is to peacefully oppose or try to improve government proposals.

q: What is Elections Canada?
opts: A federal department within the government that sets and manages election dates
An independent, neutral agency of Parliament that manages elections and maintains voters' lists
A regulatory body that reviews and approves the eligibility of election candidates
A parliamentary committee that oversees the counting of ballots after each election
exp: The voters' lists used during federal elections and referendums are produced from the National Register of Electors by a neutral agency of Parliament called Elections Canada. This is a permanent database of Canadian citizens 18 years of age or older who are qualified to vote.

q: How do you mark a ballot in a federal election?
opts: Write the full legal name of your preferred candidate on the ballot
Place an X in the circle beside the name of your chosen candidate
Rank all candidates on the ballot from most to least preferred
Touch the screen on an electronic voting machine to select your candidate
exp: You mark your ballot by placing an 'X' in the circle next to the name of the candidate of your choice.

q: What are the three major political parties currently represented in the House of Commons according to the study guide?
opts: The Liberal Party, the NDP, and the Green Party
The Conservative Party, the New Democratic Party, and the Liberal Party
The Liberal Party, the Bloc Québécois, and the Green Party
The Conservative Party, the Liberal Party, and the Bloc Québécois
exp: The study guide states there are three major political parties currently represented in the House of Commons: the Conservative Party, the New Democratic Party, and the Liberal Party.

q: What is an advance poll?
opts: A public opinion poll that predicts the election result
An opportunity to vote before the official election day if needed
A special vote held exclusively for senior citizens
A backup vote held in case the main election is cancelled
exp: If you cannot or do not wish to vote on election day, you can vote at the advance polls or by special ballot. The dates and location are on your voter information card.

q: What happens if a majority of House of Commons members vote against a major government decision?
opts: The Senate may override the House of Commons and reverse the decision
The government falls and the Prime Minister typically must call a new election
The Governor General immediately appoints a new Prime Minister from the opposition
The Supreme Court intervenes to resolve the resulting constitutional crisis
exp: If a majority of the members of the House of Commons vote against a major government decision such as the budget, the party in power is defeated, which usually results in the Prime Minister asking the Governor General, on behalf of the Sovereign, to call an election.

q: Who can run as a candidate in a federal election?
opts: Only members of registered political parties
Canadian citizens who are 18 years old or older
Any permanent resident who has lived in Canada for 5 years
Only Canadian-born citizens aged 21 and over
exp: Canadian citizens who are 18 years old or older may run in a federal election. The people who run for office are called candidates. There can be many candidates in an electoral district.

q: What does the Cabinet do?
opts: The Cabinet introduces all new legislation without prior approval from the House
The PM and Cabinet direct the government, prepare the budget, and propose new laws
The Cabinet controls Senate appointments and directly selects all federal court judges
The Cabinet is responsible for the daily administrative operations of Parliament
exp: The Prime Minister and the Cabinet ministers are called the Cabinet and they make important decisions about how the country is governed. They prepare the budget and propose most new laws. Their decisions can be questioned by all members of the House of Commons.

q: In Canada, are you obliged to tell other people how you voted?
opts: Yes, you must disclose your vote to your employer if asked
Yes, you must publicly declare your vote if a court requests it
No — you may choose to share how you voted, but no one can demand you tell them
Yes, but only to immediate family members
exp: You may choose to discuss how you voted with others, but no one — including family members, your employer or union representative — has the right to insist that you tell them how you voted. The ballot is secret.

q: What is the presumption of innocence in Canada?
opts: All accused persons bear the burden of proving their own innocence in court
Every person charged with an offence is considered innocent until proven guilty in court
Police treat all suspects as guilty unless and until evidence proves otherwise
The presumption applies only to first-time offenders charged with minor offences
exp: The Canadian justice system guarantees everyone due process under the law. Our judicial system is founded on the presumption of innocence in criminal matters, meaning everyone is innocent until proven guilty.

q: What is due process in Canada?
opts: The specific steps that police must follow to make an arrest
The principle that the government must respect all legal rights a person is entitled to
The formal process of applying for Canadian citizenship
The time limit for bringing a criminal case to court
exp: Due process is the principle that the government must respect all the legal rights a person is entitled to under the law. Canada's legal system is based on a heritage that includes the rule of law, freedom under the law, democratic principles and due process.

q: What is the Supreme Court of Canada?
opts: A court that handles only criminal cases across Canada
Canada's highest court — the Federal Court deals with matters concerning the federal government
A court that only hears cases involving the federal government
The court that must approve all legislation passed by Parliament
exp: The Supreme Court of Canada is our country's highest court. The Federal Court of Canada deals with matters concerning the federal government. In most provinces there is an appeal court and a trial court, sometimes called the Court of Queen's Bench or the Supreme Court.

q: What is the role of the police in Canada?
opts: To create and enforce all laws across Canada at every level of government
To enforce federal laws exclusively, leaving provincial matters to other agencies
To keep people safe, enforce the law, and serve communities who may question their conduct
To serve the federal government only, with no duty to assist the public directly
exp: The police are there to keep people safe and to enforce the law. You can ask the police for help in all kinds of situations. You can also question the police about their service or conduct if you feel you need to. Almost all police forces in Canada have a process by which you can bring your concerns to the police and seek action.

q: What are the different types of police in Canada?
opts: Only the RCMP operates anywhere in Canada
Canada has only one national police force — the RCMP
Each province has its own separate federal police force
Ontario and Quebec have provincial police; the RCMP enforces federal laws and serves other provinces
exp: There are different types of police in Canada. There are provincial police forces in Ontario and Quebec and municipal police departments in all provinces. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) enforce federal laws throughout Canada, and serve as the provincial police in all provinces and territories except Ontario and Quebec, as well as in some municipalities.

q: What are legal aid services in Canada?
opts: Government prosecutors who represent the Crown in criminal trials
Free or subsidized legal services available in most communities for those who cannot afford a lawyer
A government fund used to finance police investigations and court proceedings
Legal services available only to Canadian citizens, not permanent residents or newcomers
exp: Lawyers can help you with legal problems and act for you in court. If you cannot pay for a lawyer, in most communities there are legal aid services available free of charge or at a low cost.

q: When was the current Canadian flag first raised?
exp: A new Canadian flag was raised for the first time in 1965. The red-white-red pattern comes from the flag of the Royal Military College, Kingston, founded in 1876. Red and white had been colours of France and England since the Middle Ages and the national colours of Canada since 1921.

q: When did Canada adopt red and white as its national colours?
exp: Red and white had been colours of France and England since the Middle Ages and the national colours of Canada since 1921.

q: What is Canada's national motto and what does it mean?
opts: 'Peace, Order and Good Government' — meaning Canada is governed peacefully
'A mari usque ad mare' — Latin meaning 'from sea to sea'
'True North Strong and Free' — meaning Canada is a northern nation
'O Canada' — meaning our home and native land
exp: Canada adopted an official coat of arms and a national motto, A mari usque ad mare, which in Latin means 'from sea to sea.' The arms contain symbols of England, France, Scotland and Ireland as well as red maple leaves.

q: What is Canada's national anthem and when was it proclaimed?
opts: 'God Save the King' — proclaimed in 1867
'O Canada' — proclaimed national anthem in 1980, first sung in Quebec City in 1880
'The Maple Leaf Forever' — proclaimed as the anthem in 1900
'True North' — proclaimed as national anthem in 1982
exp: O Canada was proclaimed as the national anthem in 1980. It was first sung in Quebec City in 1880. French and English Canadians sing different words to the national anthem.

q: What is Canada's official summer sport?
opts: Baseball
Soccer
Lacrosse
Football
exp: Lacrosse, an ancient sport first played by Aboriginals, is the official summer sport. Hockey is Canada's most popular spectator sport and is considered to be the national winter sport.

q: What is Canada's national winter sport?
opts: Curling
Skiing
Speed skating
Ice hockey
exp: Hockey is Canada's most popular spectator sport and is considered to be the national winter sport. Ice hockey was developed in Canada in the 1800s.

q: What coin does the beaver appear on?
opts: The penny (one-cent coin)
The nickel (five-cent coin)
The dime (ten-cent coin)
The quarter (twenty-five-cent coin)
exp: The industrious beaver can be seen on the five-cent coin, on the coats of arms of Saskatchewan and Alberta, and of cities such as Montreal and Toronto. The beaver was adopted centuries ago as a symbol of the Hudson's Bay Company.

q: When was the Peace Tower completed and what does it contain?
opts: Completed in 1867 to mark Confederation — contains the Senate chamber
Completed in 1927 in memory of WWI — the Memorial Chamber holds the Books of Remembrance
Completed in 1965 when the new Canadian flag was first raised
Completed in 1982 to mark the patriation of the Constitution
exp: The Peace Tower was completed in 1927 in memory of the First World War. The Memorial Chamber within the Tower contains the Books of Remembrance in which are written the names of soldiers, sailors and airmen who died serving Canada in wars or while on duty.

q: What is the Order of Canada and when was it started?
opts: Canada's highest military honour, started in 1945
Canada's own honours system started in 1967, the centennial of Confederation
A medal given to all new Canadian citizens since 1982
An award for outstanding athletes, started in 1971
exp: After using British honours for many years, Canada started its own honours system with the Order of Canada in 1967, the centennial of Confederation.

q: What is the Victoria Cross?
opts: Canada's medal for 25 years of service in the Armed Forces
The highest honour for Canadians — awarded for conspicuous bravery facing the enemy — 96 awarded since 1854
A medal given to all Canadian veterans of the Second World War
An honour awarded by the Governor General to outstanding civilians
exp: The Victoria Cross (V.C.) is the highest honour available to Canadians and is awarded for the most conspicuous bravery, a daring or pre-eminent act of valour or self-sacrifice, or extreme devotion to duty in the presence of the enemy. The V.C. has been awarded to 96 Canadians since 1854.

q: What is the Royal Anthem of Canada?
opts: O Canada
The Maple Leaf Forever
God Save the Queen (or King)
True North
exp: The Royal Anthem of Canada, 'God Save the Queen (or King),' can be played or sung on any occasion when Canadians wish to honour the Sovereign.

q: What is Remembrance Day and when is it observed?
opts: A national holiday on November 1 to honour all living Canadian veterans
Observed on November 11 — Canadians wear red poppies and observe silence at the 11th hour
A national holiday on the second Monday of November to celebrate world peace
Observed on June 6 each year to mark the anniversary of the D-Day landings
exp: Canadians remember the sacrifices of veterans and brave fallen each year on November 11: Remembrance Day. Canadians wear the red poppy and observe a moment of silence at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month to honour the sacrifices of over a million brave men and women who have served, and the 110,000 who have given their lives.

q: What are Canada's national public holidays? When is Canada Day?
opts: Canada Day is June 24
Canada Day is July 1
Canada Day is July 4
Canada Day is September 1
exp: Canada Day is July 1 — celebrating the birth of Canada on July 1, 1867. Other national public holidays include New Year's Day (January 1), Good Friday, Victoria Day (Monday preceding May 25), Labour Day (first Monday of September), Thanksgiving Day (second Monday of October), Remembrance Day (November 11), and Christmas Day (December 25).

q: Canada has one of the world's largest economies — what group does it belong to?
opts: The G5
The G7
The G8
The G20 only
exp: Today, Canada has one of the ten largest economies in the world and is part of the G8 group of leading industrialized countries with the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, France, Japan and Russia.

q: What are the three main types of industries in Canada's economy?
opts: Technology, manufacturing industries, and agriculture
Service industries, manufacturing industries, and natural resources industries
Energy, forestry, and commercial fishing industries
Banking, international trade, and tourism industries
exp: Canada's economy includes three main types of industries: service industries (transportation, education, health care, banking, etc.), manufacturing industries (paper, automobiles, aerospace, etc.), and natural resources industries (forestry, fishing, agriculture, mining and energy).

q: What percentage of working Canadians have jobs in service industries?
opts: About 50%
About 60%
More than 75%
About 90%
exp: Service industries provide thousands of different jobs in areas like transportation, education, health care, construction, banking, communications, retail services, tourism and government. More than 75% of working Canadians now have jobs in service industries.

q: Who is Canada's largest international trading partner?
opts: China
The United Kingdom
The United States
Mexico
exp: Canada's largest international trading partner is the United States. Over three-quarters of Canadian exports are destined for the U.S.A. Canada and the U.S. have the biggest bilateral trading relationship in the world.

q: When did Canada enact free trade with the United States?
exp: In 1988, Canada enacted free trade with the United States. Mexico became a partner in 1994 in the broader North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).

q: How many provinces and territories does Canada have?
opts: 8 provinces and 2 territories
10 provinces and 3 territories
12 provinces and 1 territory
9 provinces and 4 territories
exp: Canada has ten provinces and three territories. Each province and territory has its own capital city.

q: What is Canada's population approximately?
opts: About 25 million
About 30 million
About 34 million
About 40 million
exp: Canada has a population of about 34 million people. While the majority live in cities, Canadians also live in small towns, rural areas and everywhere in between.

q: Why was Ottawa chosen as Canada's capital and when?
opts: Ottawa was chosen as the capital in 1857 by Queen Victoria
It was chosen in 1867 because it was the largest Canadian city
It was chosen in 1864 at the Charlottetown Conference
Parliament moved to Ottawa in 1871 after British Columbia joined
exp: Ottawa, located on the Ottawa River, was chosen as the capital in 1857 by Queen Victoria. Today it is Canada's fourth largest metropolitan area.

q: What are Canada's five regions?
opts: North, South, East, West, and Central
The Atlantic Provinces, Central Canada, The Prairie Provinces, The West Coast, and The Northern Territories
Quebec, Ontario, the Prairies, British Columbia, and the Arctic
The Maritimes, Central Canada, the Rockies, the Pacific Coast, and the Territories
exp: Canada includes many different geographical areas and five distinct regions: The Atlantic Provinces, Central Canada, The Prairie Provinces, The West Coast, and The Northern Territories.

q: What are the Atlantic Provinces?
opts: Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick
Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick
Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, and Prince Edward Island
New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Manitoba
exp: The Atlantic Provinces are Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick. Atlantic Canada's coasts and natural resources, including fishing, farming, forestry and mining, have made these provinces an important part of Canada's history and development.

q: What is Prince Edward Island known for?
opts: Known for large-scale oil production and its thriving energy industry
Known for its technology sector and status as a major Canadian financial centre
Known for its large Indigenous population and vast northern wilderness landscape
The smallest province, known for red soil, beaches, farming, and as the birthplace of Confederation
exp: Prince Edward Island (P.E.I.) is the smallest province, known for its beaches, red soil and agriculture, especially potatoes. P.E.I. is the birthplace of Confederation, connected to mainland Canada by one of the longest continuous multispan bridges in the world, the Confederation Bridge. Anne of Green Gables, set in P.E.I. by Lucy Maud Montgomery, is a much-loved story.

q: What is Central Canada and what does it produce?
opts: Manitoba and Saskatchewan — known for wheat and grain farming
Ontario and Quebec — half of all Canadians live here; produce three-quarters of all manufactured goods
Alberta and British Columbia — known for energy and forestry
Nova Scotia and New Brunswick — known for fishing and shipbuilding
exp: More than half the people in Canada live in cities and towns near the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River in southern Quebec and Ontario, known as Central Canada and the industrial and manufacturing heartland. Together, Ontario and Quebec produce more than three-quarters of all Canadian manufactured goods.

q: What are the Prairie Provinces and what are they known for?
opts: British Columbia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan — known for mountains and offshore oil
Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta — known for vast farmland and major energy resources
Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Ontario — known for grain farming and heavy manufacturing
Alberta, Saskatchewan, and the Northwest Territories — known for oil and gas extraction
exp: Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are the Prairie Provinces, rich in energy resources and some of the most fertile farmland in the world. The region is mostly dry, with cold winters and hot summers.

q: What is Saskatchewan's contribution to Canada's agriculture?
opts: Canada's leading dairy-producing province, with the largest number of dairy farms
Home to 40% of Canada's farmland, leading in grains, oilseeds, uranium, and potash
Canada's largest producer of beef cattle and the top exporter of red meat
The top producer of Canadian fruit, wine grapes, and orchard crops
exp: Saskatchewan, once known as the 'breadbasket of the world' and the 'wheat province,' has 40% of the arable land in Canada and is the country's largest producer of grains and oilseeds. It also boasts the world's richest deposits of uranium and potash, used in fertilizer, and produces oil and natural gas.

q: What is the RCMP training academy located in and what city?
opts: In Alberta — located in Calgary
In Ontario — located in Ottawa
In Saskatchewan — located in Regina, the provincial capital
In Manitoba — located in Winnipeg
exp: Regina, the capital of Saskatchewan, is home to the training academy of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

q: What is British Columbia known for?
opts: Known for flat prairie landscapes and some of Canada's largest oil refineries
Known for mountains, Pacific coastline, and Vancouver's role as Canada's main trading port
Known for its French-speaking majority and distinct civil law legal tradition
Known for being the largest Canadian province by total land area
exp: British Columbia is known for its majestic mountains and as Canada's Pacific gateway. The Port of Vancouver, Canada's largest and busiest, handles billions of dollars in goods traded around the world. Warm airstreams from the Pacific Ocean give the B.C. coast a temperate climate.

q: What is Montreal known for?
opts: The capital city of Quebec and seat of the provincial government
Canada's second-largest city and the world's second-largest French-speaking city after Paris
The city that houses Canada's federal Parliament and Supreme Court buildings
Canada's largest English-speaking city east of Toronto
exp: Montreal, Canada's second largest city and the second largest mainly French-speaking city in the world after Paris, is famous for its cultural diversity.

q: What is the largest freshwater lake in the world and where is it?
opts: Lake Ontario — the smallest of the Great Lakes, bordering Ontario and New York
Lake Superior — the largest freshwater lake in the world, one of the five Great Lakes
Lake Huron — the second-largest Great Lake, located entirely within Ontario
Great Bear Lake — Canada's largest lake, located in the Northwest Territories
exp: There are five Great Lakes located between Ontario and the United States: Lake Ontario, Lake Erie, Lake Huron, Lake Michigan (in the U.S.A.) and Lake Superior, the largest freshwater lake in the world.

q: What does 'Nunavut' mean and when was it established?
opts: 'The Arctic land' in Inuktitut — established in 1982
'Our land' in Inuktitut — established in 1999, with a population about 85% Inuit
'Northern home' in Inuktitut — established in 1993
'Land of the midnight sun' in Inuktitut — established in 2000
exp: Nunavut, meaning 'our land' in Inuktitut, was established in 1999 from the eastern part of the Northwest Territories, including all of the former District of Keewatin. The capital is Iqaluit. The population is about 85% Inuit, and Inuktitut is an official language and the first language in schools.

q: What is Nova Scotia most known for?
opts: Known for its oil sands reserves and status as a major energy-producing province
The most populous Atlantic province, known for the Bay of Fundy and Halifax's naval base
Known for its French-speaking majority and distinct Acadian cultural heritage
Known for being Canada's largest province by total geographic area
exp: Nova Scotia is the most populous Atlantic Province, with a rich history as the gateway to Canada. Known for the world's highest tides in the Bay of Fundy, the province's identity is linked to shipbuilding, fisheries and shipping. As Canada's largest east coast port, deep-water and ice-free, the capital, Halifax, has played an important role in Atlantic trade and defence and is home to Canada's largest naval base.

q: What ancient document from 1215 established the tradition of ordered liberty that Canada inherited?
opts: The Bill of Rights (1689)
The Magna Carta (Great Charter of Freedoms)
The Act of Settlement (1701)
The Declaration of Independence (1776)
exp: Canadian law secures an 800-year old tradition of ordered liberty, which dates back to the signing of Magna Carta in 1215 in England, also known as the Great Charter of Freedoms.

q: What phrase begins the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms?
opts: 'We the people of Canada affirm our common values and shared rights...'
'Whereas Canada is founded upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of law'
'All Canadians are born equal and hold these inalienable rights and freedoms...'
'Canada is a free and democratic society that upholds liberty and justice for all...'
exp: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms begins with the words, 'Whereas Canada is founded upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of law.' This phrase underlines the importance of religious traditions to Canadian society and the dignity and worth of the human person.

q: What does the Canadian Charter say about multiculturalism?
opts: Multiculturalism is a temporary policy subject to review every 10 years
Multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of Canadian heritage — Canadians celebrate diversity and live in harmony
Multiculturalism only applies to immigrants within their first 10 years
Multiculturalism requires all Canadians to learn a second language
exp: The Charter describes Multiculturalism as a fundamental characteristic of the Canadian heritage and identity. Canadians celebrate the gift of one another's presence and work hard to respect pluralism and live in harmony.

q: What can young Canadians do to serve their country besides joining the regular Canadian Forces?
opts: Nothing — serving in the regular Canadian Armed Forces is the only meaningful option
Serve in the part-time reserves, join the cadets, or volunteer in emergency services
