Apply to serve as an elections officer for Elections Canada during federal elections
Join a provincial police force only after first obtaining full Canadian citizenship
exp: You can serve in your local part-time navy, militia and air reserves and gain valuable experience, skills and contacts. Young people can learn discipline, responsibility and skills by getting involved in the cadets. You may also serve in the Coast Guard or emergency services such as a police force or fire department.

q: What were the diverse Aboriginal groups and what were their ways of life when Europeans arrived?
opts: All Aboriginal groups were nomadic hunters who followed buffalo herds across the Prairies
All Aboriginal peoples were coastal fishers who lived along the ocean shores
Huron-Wendat farmed; Cree and Dene gathered; Sioux followed bison; Inuit and West Coast peoples lived off wildlife
Aboriginal peoples lived only in the northern territories and the Prairies
exp: The native people lived off the land in diverse ways: the Huron-Wendat of the Great Lakes region, like the Iroquois, were farmers and hunters. The Cree and Dene of the Northwest were hunter-gatherers. The Sioux were nomadic, following the bison (buffalo) herd. The Inuit lived off Arctic wildlife. West Coast natives preserved fish by drying and smoking.

q: When were Aboriginal territorial rights first guaranteed and by whom?
opts: At Confederation in 1867, through legislation introduced by Sir John A. Macdonald
Through the Royal Proclamation of 1763 by King George III, establishing the basis for treaty talks
In 1982 through Section 35 of the Constitution Act, which recognized Aboriginal rights
In 1971 through the federal Multiculturalism Act and subsequent treaty agreements
exp: Aboriginal and treaty rights are in the Canadian Constitution. Territorial rights were first guaranteed through the Royal Proclamation of 1763 by King George III, and established the basis for negotiating treaties with the newcomers — treaties that were not always fully respected.

q: What impact did the arrival of European traders, missionaries, soldiers and colonists have on Aboriginal peoples?
opts: It had no significant or lasting impact on traditional Aboriginal ways of life
It changed Aboriginal life forever — disease caused great losses, but economic and cultural bonds also formed
It affected only Aboriginal communities living along the Atlantic and Pacific coastlines
It led to the immediate and total assimilation of all Aboriginal peoples within decades
exp: The arrival of European traders, missionaries, soldiers and colonists changed the native way of life forever. Large numbers of Aboriginals died of European diseases to which they lacked immunity. However, Aboriginals and Europeans formed strong economic, religious and military bonds in the first 200 years of coexistence which laid the foundations of Canada.

q: Who established the basic way of life in English-speaking areas of Canada?
opts: American settlers who migrated north following the American Revolutionary War
Hundreds of thousands of English, Welsh, Scottish, and Irish settlers who arrived from the 1600s onward
Exclusively British military soldiers who were permanently posted to garrison duty in Canada
German and Dutch settlers who began arriving in large numbers during the 1800s
exp: The basic way of life in English-speaking areas was established by hundreds of thousands of English, Welsh, Scottish and Irish settlers, soldiers and migrants from the 1600s to the 20th century. Generations of pioneers and builders of British origins, as well as other groups, invested and endured hardship in laying the foundations of our country.

q: What are the largest ethnic groups in Canada?
opts: English, French, German, Chinese, Italian, Ukrainian, and South Asian among many others
Only English and French communities, which together form the majority population
English, American, and Australian, reflecting Commonwealth cultural ties
Chinese, South Asian, and Filipino, reflecting recent immigration patterns
exp: Many ethnic and religious groups live and work in peace as proud Canadians. The largest groups are the English, French, Scottish, Irish, German, Italian, Chinese, Aboriginal, Ukrainian, Dutch, South Asian and Scandinavian. Since the 1970s, most immigrants have come from Asian countries.

q: What is the role of faith communities in Canadian society?
opts: Religion has no role whatsoever in Canadian public life
Faith communities are prohibited from providing social services
Only Christian faith communities are formally recognized by the state
The state has traditionally partnered with faith communities to promote welfare, harmony, and religious freedom
exp: In Canada the state has traditionally partnered with faith communities to promote social welfare, harmony and mutual respect; to provide schools and health care; to resettle refugees; and to uphold religious freedom, religious expression and freedom of conscience.

q: What is the Vikings' connection to Canada?
opts: Vikings were the first Europeans to formally claim and name Canada as a territory
Vikings from Iceland who settled Greenland also reached Labrador and Newfoundland around 1000 AD
Vikings established the first permanent European settlement in Canada, lasting several centuries
Vikings traded with Indigenous peoples along the coast but never permanently settled in Canada
exp: The Vikings from Iceland who colonized Greenland 1,000 years ago also reached Labrador and the island of Newfoundland. The remains of their settlement, l'Anse aux Meadows, are a World Heritage site.

q: What was the significance of the Hudson's Bay Company granted in 1670?
opts: It financed and built the first transcontinental railway linking eastern and western Canada
It was the first elected legislative assembly established in British North America
King Charles II granted it exclusive trading rights over the vast Hudson Bay watershed in 1670
It was given full administrative control over all of the territory of New France
exp: In 1670, King Charles II of England granted the Hudson's Bay Company exclusive trading rights over the watershed draining into Hudson Bay. For the next 100 years the Company competed with Montreal-based traders. The skilled and courageous men who travelled by canoe were called voyageurs and coureurs des bois.

q: Who were the voyageurs and coureurs des bois?
opts: French soldiers who defended New France against British military attacks
Skilled traders and paddlers who canoed the fur trade routes and allied with First Nations
English settlers who built the first permanent roads and bridges in Upper Canada
Missionaries who travelled inland to convert Indigenous peoples to Christianity
exp: The skilled and courageous men who travelled by canoe in the fur trade were called voyageurs and coureurs des bois. They formed strong alliances with First Nations.

q: What did Jean Talon, Bishop Laval, and Count Frontenac build in New France?
opts: The first universities and schools anywhere in North America
A French Empire in North America stretching from Hudson Bay to the Gulf of Mexico
The first permanent European settlements established along the Atlantic coast
The fur trading posts that eventually grew into modern Canadian cities
exp: Outstanding leaders like Jean Talon, Bishop Laval, and Count Frontenac built a French Empire in North America that reached from Hudson Bay to the Gulf of Mexico.

q: What did Count Frontenac famously say when asked to surrender Quebec to the English in 1690?
opts: 'Quebec shall never fall to the English!'
'My only reply will be from the mouths of my cannons!'
'France will never abandon her colony!'
'We shall fight to the very last man!'
exp: Count Frontenac refused to surrender Quebec to the English in 1690, saying: 'My only reply will be from the mouths of my cannons!'

q: What was the Great Peace of Montreal of 1701?
opts: A peace treaty between Canada and the United States
A peace agreement that brought together 40 First Nations to end conflicts
A trade agreement between New France and the British colonies
A religious agreement between Catholics and Protestants in Canada
exp: The Great Peace of Montreal of 1701 brought together 40 First Nations to end conflicts.

q: What was the Montreal Stock Exchange and when did it open?
opts: Canada's first chartered bank, opened in 1792
The first financial institution in Canada, opened in 1832
A colonial trading post for the fur trade, opened in the 1700s
A government financial institution opened after Confederation
exp: The Montreal Stock Exchange opened in 1832. The first financial institutions opened in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.

q: Who was Mary Ann Shadd Cary and what was her significance?
opts: Canada's first female Prime Minister
An anti-slavery activist who in 1853 became the first woman publisher in Canada, co-founding The Provincial Freeman
The first woman elected to the House of Commons in 1921
A Famous Five member who fought for women to be recognized as persons
exp: Mary Ann Shadd Cary was an outspoken activist in the movement to abolish slavery in the U.S.A. In 1853 she became the first woman publisher in Canada, helping to found and edit The Provincial Freeman, a weekly newspaper dedicated to anti-slavery, black immigration to Canada, temperance and upholding British rule.

q: What was the Underground Railroad?
opts: A secret tunnel system under Montreal used during the American Civil War
A Christian anti-slavery network through which thousands of slaves escaped the US and settled in Canada
A network of French settlers who helped Loyalists escape to Canada
A system for transporting mail and goods across Upper Canada
exp: Thousands of slaves escaped from the United States, followed 'the North Star' and settled in Canada via the Underground Railroad, a Christian anti-slavery network.

q: What happened to some Nova Scotians who were given poor land after coming to Canada as Loyalists?
opts: They returned to the United States permanently
In 1792, some moved to establish Freetown, Sierra Leone — a new British colony for freed slaves
They moved to Upper Canada and settled near the Great Lakes
They petitioned the British government for better land in the West Indies
exp: In turn, in 1792, some Nova Scotians who were given poor land moved on to establish Freetown, Sierra Leone (West Africa), a new British colony for freed slaves.

q: What was the Rebellions of 1837–38?
opts: A successful revolution that led to Canada's immediate independence from Britain
Armed uprisings in Upper and Lower Canada demanding faster democratic reform, defeated by British troops
A border war fought between Canada and the United States along the Niagara frontier
An Indigenous-led uprising against European settler expansion in the Prairie West
exp: In the 1830s, reformers in Upper and Lower Canada believed that progress toward full democracy was too slow. When armed rebellions occurred in 1837–38, the rebels did not have enough public support to succeed. They were defeated by British troops and Canadian volunteers. A number of rebels were hanged or exiled.

q: Who was Lord Durham and what did he recommend after the 1837–38 rebellions?
opts: A Canadian reformer who advocated for full independence from British rule
An English reformer who recommended merging the Canadas, granting responsible government, and French assimilation
The Governor General who personally commanded troops to suppress the 1837 rebellions
A British general who decisively defeated the rebel forces in both Upper and Lower Canada
exp: Lord Durham, an English reformer sent to report on the rebellions, recommended that Upper and Lower Canada be merged and given responsible government. Controversially, Lord Durham also said that the quickest way for the Canadiens to achieve progress was to assimilate into English-speaking Protestant culture — a recommendation that demonstrated a complete lack of understanding of French Canadians.

q: Who was Sir Louis-Hippolyte La Fontaine?
opts: Canada's very first Prime Minister, serving from Confederation until 1873
A champion of democracy and French rights who led responsible government in the Canadas in 1849
The principal Father of Confederation who represented Quebec at the 1864 conferences
The founder of the modern Bloc Québécois and Quebec sovereignty movement
exp: Sir Louis-Hippolyte La Fontaine was a champion of democracy and French language rights. He became the first leader of a responsible government (similar to a prime minister) in the Canadas in 1849.

q: What was Sir George-Étienne Cartier's role in Confederation?
opts: The first Premier of Quebec, elected after Confederation in 1867
A key architect of Confederation from Quebec who helped bring western provinces into Canada
The co-founder of the Liberal Party of Canada alongside Sir Wilfrid Laurier
The chief Canadian negotiator of the 1763 Treaty of Paris with France
exp: Sir George-Étienne Cartier was the key architect of Confederation from Quebec. A railway lawyer, Montrealer, close ally of Macdonald and patriotic Canadien, Cartier led Quebec into Confederation and helped negotiate the entry of the Northwest Territories, Manitoba and British Columbia into Canada.

q: Whose portrait is on the Canadian $10 bill?
opts: Sir Wilfrid Laurier
Sir Robert Borden
Sir John A. Macdonald
Sir Georges-Étienne Cartier
exp: Sir John A. Macdonald's portrait is on the $10 bill. Parliament has recognized January 11 as Sir John A. Macdonald Day.

q: Whose portrait is on the Canadian $5 bill?
opts: Sir John A. Macdonald
Sir Wilfrid Laurier
Sir Robert Borden
Louis Riel
exp: Sir Wilfrid Laurier's portrait is on the $5 bill. He was the first French-Canadian prime minister since Confederation and encouraged immigration to the West.

q: What was the North West Mounted Police (NWMP) established to do?
opts: To protect the Canadian Pacific Railway from sabotage during construction in the West
Established in 1873 to bring order to the West and assist in treaty negotiations with Indigenous peoples
To enforce the Chinese Head Tax once the CPR was fully completed in 1885
To patrol and secure the Canada-United States border established after the War of 1812
exp: Prime Minister Macdonald established the North West Mounted Police (NWMP) in 1873 to pacify the West and assist in negotiations with the Indians. The NWMP founded Fort Calgary, Fort MacLeod and other centres that today are cities and towns. Regina became its headquarters.

q: Who was Major-General Sir Sam Steele?
opts: The first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada after Confederation
One of Canada's most celebrated frontier heroes — a distinguished Mounted Policeman and soldier
The general who commanded all Canadian forces during the Battle of Vimy Ridge
The founding commander of the Royal Canadian Air Force in the 1920s
exp: Some of Canada's most colourful heroes, such as Major-General Sir Sam Steele, came from the ranks of the Mounties. He is described as a great frontier hero, Mounted Policeman and soldier of the Queen.

q: Who was Joseph Brant and what did he do?
opts: A French-Canadian general who fought at Vimy Ridge
Joseph Brant led thousands of Loyalist Mohawk Indians into Canada during the American Revolution
A Métis leader who led the Red River Resistance against Ottawa
The first Indigenous member elected to the Canadian Parliament
exp: Joseph Brant led thousands of Loyalist Mohawk Indians into Canada. The Loyalists came from Dutch, German, British, Scandinavian, Aboriginal and other origins and from Presbyterian, Anglican, Baptist, Methodist, Jewish, Quaker and Catholic religious backgrounds.

q: What was Donald Smith's (Lord Strathcona's) role in completing the CPR?
opts: He was the engineer who designed the entire railway route
The Scottish-born CPR director who drove the last spike on November 7, 1885
He was the Prime Minister who authorized and funded the CPR
He led the Chinese workers on the most difficult mountain section
exp: On November 7, 1885, a powerful symbol of unity was completed when Donald Smith (Lord Strathcona), the Scottish-born director of the Canadian Pacific Railway (CPR), drove the last spike.

q: How many Ukrainians, Poles and other immigrants settled in the West before 1914 thanks to the railway?
opts: About 50,000 Ukrainians and 30,000 Poles settled in Western Canada before 1914
170,000 Ukrainians, 115,000 Poles, and tens of thousands from Germany, Norway, and Sweden
Approximately 500,000 immigrants from all European countries combined before 1914
Around 100,000 Ukrainians and 50,000 Poles settled in the Prairie West before 1914
exp: The railway made it possible for immigrants, including 170,000 Ukrainians, 115,000 Poles and tens of thousands from Germany, France, Norway and Sweden to settle in the West before 1914 and develop a thriving agricultural sector.

q: What happened to Austro-Hungarian subjects in Canada during World War I?
opts: They were welcomed as valued allies in Canada's effort against the German Empire
Over 8,000 Austro-Hungarian subjects were interned as 'enemy aliens' in 24 labour camps
They were promptly deported back to Austria-Hungary at the start of the war
They were conscripted directly into the Canadian military to serve on the Western Front
exp: Regrettably, from 1914 to 1920, Ottawa interned over 8,000 former Austro-Hungarian subjects, mainly Ukrainian men, as 'enemy aliens' in 24 labour camps across Canada, even though Britain advised against the policy.

q: Who was General Sir Arthur Currie?
opts: Canada's first Minister of National Defence, appointed after the First World War
A reserve officer who became Canada's greatest WWI commander, leading key victories in the last hundred days
The general who personally commanded the Canadian assault brigades on D-Day
The founding commander of the Royal Canadian Air Force established in the 1920s
exp: In 1918, under the command of General Sir Arthur Currie, Canada's greatest soldier, the Canadian Corps advanced alongside the French and British Empire troops in the last hundred days. These included the victorious Battle of Amiens on August 8, 1918 — which the Germans called 'the black day of the German Army' — followed by Arras, Canal du Nord, Cambrai and Mons.

q: What poem is often recited on Remembrance Day and who wrote it?
opts: 'The Maple Leaf Forever' — written by Alexander Muir
'In Flanders Fields' — written by Canadian Lieutenant-Colonel John McCrae in 1915
'O Canada' — composed by Calixa Lavallée
'The Soldier' — written by British poet Rupert Brooke
exp: Canadian medical officer Lieutenant-Colonel John McCrae composed the poem 'In Flanders Fields' in 1915; it is often recited on Remembrance Day.

q: What was the 'Roaring Twenties' and what followed?
opts: A period of wartime hardship followed by economic recovery and renewed prosperity
Boom times with high employment and prosperity, followed by the 1929 crash and the Great Depression
A cultural revolution in Quebec followed by a push for French-Canadian independence
A wave of mass immigration followed by new federal restrictions on new arrivals
exp: The 'Roaring Twenties' were boom times, with prosperity for businesses and low unemployment. The stock market crash of 1929, however, led to the Great Depression or the 'Dirty Thirties.' Unemployment reached 27% in 1933 and many businesses were wiped out. Farmers in Western Canada were hit hardest by low grain prices and a terrible drought.

q: When was the Bank of Canada created and what is its purpose?
opts: Created in 1867 at Confederation to finance the newly formed Canadian government
Created in 1934 as Canada's central bank to manage the money supply and stabilize finance
Created in 1945 to rebuild the Canadian economy after the Second World War
Created in 1982 when the Constitution was patriated from the British Parliament
exp: The Bank of Canada, a central bank to manage the money supply and bring stability to the financial system, was created in 1934.

q: What was the Royal Canadian Air Force's contribution in World War II?
opts: It flew all of the D-Day air support missions exclusively over Normandy
It served exclusively in the Pacific theatre fighting Japanese forces until 1945
It fought in the Battle of Britain and led Commonwealth nations in Allied air power
It was formed specifically to bomb German oil refineries in occupied Europe
exp: The Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) took part in the Battle of Britain and provided a high proportion of Commonwealth aircrew in bombers and fighter planes over Europe. Canada contributed more to the Allied air effort than any other Commonwealth country, with over 130,000 Allied air crew trained in Canada under the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan.

q: What was the Battle of Amiens (August 8, 1918) known as?
opts: 'The greatest single Canadian military victory of the entire First World War'
'The black day of the German Army' — a decisive victory led by the Canadian Corps
'The turning point of the entire Western Front and the beginning of the end'
'The day Canada proved its military worth to the British Empire'
exp: The victorious Battle of Amiens on August 8, 1918 — which the Germans called 'the black day of the German Army' — was one of the key victories in the last hundred days of WWI led by the Canadian Corps under General Sir Arthur Currie.

q: What was the women's suffrage movement in Canada?
opts: A movement for women's equal pay in the workplace, active mainly in the 1960s
The effort to win women the right to vote, founded by Dr. Emily Stowe; Manitoba was first in 1916
A movement for women's labour rights and workplace safety, prominent in the 1950s
A campaign founded by Agnes Macphail to elect more women to Parliament
exp: The effort by women to achieve the right to vote is known as the women's suffrage movement. Its founder in Canada was Dr. Emily Stowe, the first Canadian woman to practise medicine in Canada. In 1916, Manitoba became the first province to grant voting rights to women.

q: When did Quebec grant women the vote?
exp: Due to the work of Thérèse Casgrain and others, Quebec granted women the vote in 1940 — the last province to do so.

q: What was the Battle of Hong Kong (1941) and Dieppe (1942)?
opts: Two successful Canadian operations — one in Asia and one in Europe
Two battles where Canada defeated Japan and Germany respectively
Two peacekeeping operations that Canada led in Asia and Europe
Brave but unsuccessful Canadian operations — failed defence of Hong Kong and a failed raid on Dieppe
exp: The Canadians fought bravely and suffered losses in the unsuccessful defence of Hong Kong (1941) from attack by Imperial Japan, and in a failed raid on Nazi-controlled Dieppe on the coast of France (1942).

q: What happened at the end of WWII in the Pacific?
opts: Canada signed a formal peace treaty with Japan in Ottawa following the surrender
Canadian forces participated in the liberation of the Philippines from Japanese occupation
Canada assisted the United States in dropping atomic bombs on Japanese cities
Japan attacked Canadian territory and mistreated POWs; Japan surrendered on August 14, 1945
exp: In the Pacific war, Japan invaded the Aleutian Islands, attacked a lighthouse on Vancouver Island, launched fire balloons over B.C. and the Prairies, and grossly maltreated Canadian prisoners of war captured at Hong Kong. Japan surrendered on August 14, 1945 — the end of four years of war in the Pacific.

q: What was the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan?
opts: A Commonwealth plan to train Canadian pilots at Royal Air Force bases in Britain
Over 130,000 Allied aircrew trained in Canada, making it the top Commonwealth air training contributor
A post-war program to train commercial pilots for the expanding aviation industry
A Commonwealth agreement to share aircraft manufacturing equally between member nations
exp: Canada contributed more to the Allied air effort than any other Commonwealth country, with over 130,000 Allied air crew trained in Canada under the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan.

q: Who was Alexander Graham Bell and what is his Canadian connection?
opts: A Canadian inventor who created the telephone in his Ottawa laboratory
He conceived the idea of the telephone at his summer house in Canada
A British scientist who first demonstrated the telephone in Canada
A Canadian who commercialized the telephone after Bell invented it
exp: Alexander Graham Bell hit on the idea of the telephone at his summer house in Canada.

q: What did Matthew Evans and Henry Woodward invent?
opts: The radio transmitter, later developed commercially by Guglielmo Marconi
The first electric light bulb, a patent later sold to Thomas Edison for commercialization
The telephone, a patent held by Alexander Graham Bell of Brantford, Ontario
The snowmobile, a winter vehicle patented by Joseph-Armand Bombardier of Quebec
exp: Matthew Evans and Henry Woodward together invented the first electric light bulb and later sold the patent to Thomas Edison who, more famously, commercialized the light bulb.

q: What did Reginald Fessenden contribute?
opts: He invented the snowmobile for use in the remote Canadian winter landscape
He pioneered radio technology and sent the first wireless voice transmission in history
He invented the cardiac pacemaker used to regulate irregular heartbeats
He designed the Canadarm robotic arm used aboard the Space Shuttle
exp: Reginald Fessenden contributed to the invention of radio, sending the first wireless voice message in the world.

q: Who was Dr. Wilder Penfield and what was he known as?
opts: The Canadian inventor of the cardiac pacemaker, developed in Toronto
A pioneering brain surgeon at McGill University, called 'the greatest living Canadian'
The Montreal scientist who co-discovered insulin with Charles Best
The Halifax-born founder of the Canadian Space Agency
exp: Dr. Wilder Penfield was a pioneering brain surgeon at McGill University in Montreal, and was known as 'the greatest living Canadian.'

q: Who invented the Canadarm?
opts: Developed entirely by the National Research Council with federal funding
Built by SPAR Aerospace and the National Research Council for use in outer space
Designed by NASA engineers in partnership with the Canadian federal government
Created by the Canadian Space Agency, which was established in 1989
exp: SPAR Aerospace and the National Research Council invented the Canadarm, a robotic arm used in outer space.

q: Who were Mike Lazaridis and Jim Balsillie?
opts: The founders of the Canadian Space Agency
Of Research in Motion (RIM) — the wireless company known for inventing the BlackBerry
The inventors of the snowmobile and standard time zones respectively
Canadian Nobel Prize-winning scientists in chemistry
exp: Mike Lazaridis and Jim Balsillie of Research in Motion (RIM) — a wireless communications company known for its most famous invention: the BlackBerry.

q: Who were the Canadian Nobel Prize-winning scientists mentioned in the guide?
opts: Frederick Banting, Charles Best, Alexander Fleming, and Wilder Penfield
Gerhard Herzberg, John Polanyi, Sidney Altman, Richard Taylor, Michael Smith, and Bertram Brockhouse
Only Frederick Banting, awarded the prize for the discovery of insulin in 1923
Marshall McLuhan, Harold Innis, and Northrop Frye for contributions to communications theory
exp: Gerhard Herzberg (a refugee from Nazi Germany), John Polanyi, Sidney Altman, Richard E. Taylor, Michael Smith and Bertram Brockhouse were Nobel Prize-winning scientists mentioned in the guide.

q: What was Paul Henderson's famous achievement in 1972?
opts: He won Canada's first Olympic gold medal in ice hockey at the 1972 Winter Games
He scored the winning goal in the 1972 Canada-Soviet Summit Series, called 'the goal heard around the world'
He became the first Canadian captain to lead his team to a Stanley Cup victory
He set a new world record for goals scored in a single NHL regular season
exp: In 1972, Paul Henderson scored the winning goal for Canada in the Canada-Soviet Summit Series. This goal is often referred to as 'the goal heard around the world' and is still remembered today as an important event in both sports and cultural history.

q: What did Donovan Bailey achieve at the 1996 Olympics?
opts: He won a gold medal in ice hockey at the 1996 Atlanta Summer Olympics
He won double Olympic gold and set a world record in the 100m sprint at the 1996 Atlanta Games
He won gold in swimming and set a new world record at the 1996 Olympics
He became Canada's first gold medallist at the Paralympic Summer Games
exp: In 1996 at the Olympic Summer Games, Donovan Bailey became a world record sprinter and double Olympic gold medallist.

q: Who is Chantal Petitclerc?
opts: Canada's first female Olympic gold medallist
A world champion wheelchair racer and Paralympic gold medalist
A Canadian figure skater who won multiple world championships
A Canadian marathon runner who competed in the Olympics
exp: Chantal Petitclerc became a world champion wheelchair racer and Paralympic gold medalist.

q: What was the first Victoria Cross awarded to a Canadian and who received it?
opts: Lieutenant Billy Bishop, awarded the V.C. for aerial combat during the First World War
Lieutenant Alexander Roberts Dunn of Toronto, awarded the V.C. for the Charge of the Light Brigade in 1854
Corporal Filip Konowal, awarded the V.C. for destroying enemy machine gun positions in WWI
Able Seaman William Hall, awarded the V.C. for his actions during the Indian Rebellion
exp: Then Lieutenant Alexander Roberts Dunn, born in present-day Toronto, served in the British Army in the Charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava (1854) in the Crimean War, and was the first Canadian to be awarded the Victoria Cross.

q: Who was the first black person to be awarded the Victoria Cross?
opts: Colonel Alexander Roberts Dunn, decorated for service during the Crimean War
Able Seaman William Hall of Nova Scotia, whose parents were escaped slaves, awarded the V.C. in 1857
Corporal Filip Konowal, awarded the V.C. for bravery in the First World War
Captain Paul Triquet, awarded the V.C. for gallantry during the Second World War
exp: Able Seaman William Hall of Horton, Nova Scotia, whose parents were American slaves, was the first black man to be awarded the V.C. for his role in the Siege of Lucknow during the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

q: Who was the last Canadian to receive the Victoria Cross?
opts: Captain Paul Triquet, awarded the V.C. for actions in Italy during the Second World War
Lieutenant Robert Hampton Gray, a naval pilot from B.C., killed bombing a Japanese warship in August 1945
Flying ace Captain Billy Bishop, awarded the V.C. for aerial combat in WWI
Corporal Filip Konowal, awarded the V.C. for destroying enemy positions in WWI
exp: Lieutenant Robert Hampton Gray, a navy pilot born in Trail, B.C., was killed while bombing and sinking a Japanese warship in August 1945, a few days before the end of the Second World War, and was the last Canadian to receive the V.C. to date.

q: Who were the Nobel Prize-winning scientists mentioned in the study guide?
opts: Only Frederick Banting, awarded the Nobel Prize for the discovery of insulin
Herzberg, Polanyi, Altman, Taylor, Smith, and Brockhouse — six Canadian Nobel Prize winners in science
Marshall McLuhan, Harold Innis, and Northrop Frye for contributions to communications theory
Emily Carr, Tom Thomson, and members of the Group of Seven for contributions to art
exp: Gerhard Herzberg, a refugee from Nazi Germany, John Polanyi, Sidney Altman, Richard E. Taylor, Michael Smith and Bertram Brockhouse were Nobel Prize-winning scientists mentioned in the guide.

q: Who were Marshall McLuhan and Harold Innis?
opts: Canadian prime ministers who shaped modern Canada
Pioneer thinkers in the field of communications and technology
Canadian artists who founded the Group of Seven
Founders of the Canadian Space Agency
exp: Marshall McLuhan and Harold Innis were pioneer thinkers in the field of communications and media, mentioned in the guide as examples of Canadian advances in science and technology.

q: Which Canadian athlete was a prominent activist for gay and lesbian Canadians?
opts: Donovan Bailey
Mark Tewksbury, Olympic gold medallist
Chantal Petitclerc
Catriona Le May Doan
exp: Mark Tewksbury, Olympic gold medallist, is mentioned in the guide as a prominent activist for gay and lesbian Canadians.

q: What is the Grey Cup?
opts: The championship trophy for the National Hockey League
The championship trophy for the Canadian Football League (CFL), donated by Lord Grey in 1909
An Olympic medal awarded to outstanding Canadian athletes
An award given by the Governor General for excellence in arts
exp: Canadian football is a popular game that differs in a number of ways from American football. Professional teams in the Canadian Football League (CFL) compete for the championship Grey Cup, donated by Lord Grey, the Governor General, in 1909.

q: What refugees did Canada welcome after World War II?
opts: Only British war brides and their children, who arrived after the Allied victory
Thousands fleeing Communist oppression — 37,000 Hungarians in 1956 and over 50,000 Vietnamese after 1975
Only refugees from Western European nations displaced by wartime bombing and destruction
Exclusively Asian refugees — no European refugees were accepted in this period
exp: Canada welcomed thousands of refugees from Communist oppression, including about 37,000 who escaped Soviet tyranny in Hungary in 1956. With the Communist victory in the Vietnam War in 1975, many Vietnamese fled, including over 50,000 who sought refuge in Canada.

q: What is the significance of Les Automatistes of Quebec?
opts: A group of Quebec engineers who modernized the province's infrastructure
Pioneers of modern abstract art in the 1950s, most notably Jean-Paul Riopelle
A group of Quebec writers who fought for French language rights
The first Quebec separatist political movement in Canada
exp: Les Automatistes of Quebec were pioneers of modern abstract art in the 1950s, most notably Jean-Paul Riopelle.

q: Who was Kenojuak Ashevak?
opts: A First Nations artist from British Columbia famous for totem poles
A pioneer of modern Inuit art with etchings, prints and soapstone sculptures
A Métis artist who documented the Red River Resistance
A Quebec sculptor known for historical figure carvings
exp: Kenojuak Ashevak pioneered modern Inuit art with etchings, prints and soapstone sculptures.

q: What was the Cold War and how did Canada respond?
opts: A trade war with the Soviet Union in the 1970s
A diplomatic dispute over Arctic sovereignty with the US
When eastern Europe became Communist, Canada joined NATO and NORAD with other western democracies
A period of competition between Quebec and English Canada
exp: The Cold War began when several liberated countries of eastern Europe became part of a Communist bloc controlled by the Soviet Union under the dictator Josef Stalin. Canada joined with other democratic countries of the West to form the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), a military alliance, and with the United States in the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD).

q: What does the Sovereign's role as Head of the Commonwealth link Canada to?
opts: Only other current and former members of the British Empire
53 other nations linked through the Commonwealth for cooperation on shared global goals
Only English-speaking nations that share Canada's legal and parliamentary traditions
Only European constitutional monarchies that recognize the same sovereign
exp: As Head of the Commonwealth, the Sovereign links Canada to 53 other nations that cooperate to advance social, economic and cultural progress. Other constitutional monarchies include Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Australia, New Zealand, The Netherlands, Spain, Thailand, Japan, Jordan and Morocco.

q: What are Members of a provincial legislature called?
opts: Only MPPs — Members of the Provincial Parliament
MLAs, MNAs, MPPs, or MHAs — depending on the province or territory
They are all called Members of Parliament (MPs)
Provincial Senators appointed by the premier
exp: The members of the provincial or territorial legislature are called members of the Legislative Assembly (MLAs), members of the National Assembly (MNAs), members of the Provincial Parliament (MPPs) or members of the House of Assembly (MHAs), depending on the province or territory.

q: What is the role of the Commissioner in the territories?
opts: The Commissioner is elected by territorial citizens as their Premier
The Commissioner represents the federal government and plays a ceremonial role in the territories
The Commissioner is appointed by the Supreme Court of Canada
The Commissioner oversees federal elections in the territories
exp: In the three territories, the Commissioner represents the federal government and plays a ceremonial role.

q: What is the concept of 'Peace, Order and Good Government'?
opts: Canada's official national motto, adopted at Confederation in 1867
A key phrase in the British North America Act of 1867 describing the purpose of Canadian institutions
The guiding constitutional principle used by the Supreme Court of Canada in landmark rulings
The official motto engraved on the Governor General's seal and standard
exp: Our institutions uphold a commitment to Peace, Order and Good Government, a key phrase in Canada's original constitutional document in 1867, the British North America Act.

q: What does the First Nations band council system do?
opts: They cast votes in federal elections on behalf of all registered band members
Band chiefs and councillors manage housing, schools, and services on reserves, while organizations advocate with governments
They directly appoint Indigenous senators to represent First Nations in the Senate
They administer all federal government programs and services delivered to Indigenous communities
exp: The First Nations have band chiefs and councillors who have major responsibilities on First Nations reserves, including housing, schools and other services. There are a number of provincial, regional and national Aboriginal organizations that are a voice for First Nations, Métis and Inuit people in their relationships with the federal, provincial and territorial governments.

q: What information is on the voter information card?
opts: Only your name and home address
When and where you vote, and the number to call for interpreters or special services
A complete list of all candidates running in your riding
Your voter registration number and polling station code
exp: Once an election has been called, Elections Canada mails a voter information card to each elector. The card lists when and where you vote and the number to call if you require an interpreter or other special services.

q: What is the National Register of Electors?
opts: A list of all political parties registered in Canada
A permanent database of Canadian citizens 18 and older who are qualified to vote — maintained by Elections Canada
A list of all candidates who have ever run in a federal election
A database of all Members of Parliament since Confederation
exp: The voters' lists used during federal elections and referendums are produced from the National Register of Electors by a neutral agency of Parliament called Elections Canada. This is a permanent database of Canadian citizens 18 years of age or older who are qualified to vote in federal elections and referendums.

q: Can you still vote if you did not receive a voter information card?
opts: No — you must present a valid voter information card to be permitted to vote
Yes — you can be added to the voters' list at the polling station on election day
Only if you contact Elections Canada at least one week before the election date
Only if you can provide proof that you were previously registered to vote
exp: Even if you choose not to be listed in the National Register of Electors or do not receive a voter information card, you can still be added to the voters' list at any time, including on election day.

q: What happens immediately after polling stations close on election day?
opts: Results are announced only the following morning after a full official recount
Every ballot is counted and results are made public, viewable on TV or the Elections Canada website
The Governor General formally announces the election winner in a televised address
The winning Prime Minister is immediately sworn into office on election night
exp: When the polls close, every ballot is counted and the results are made public. You can see the results on television or on the Elections Canada website (www.elections.ca).

q: What does the blindfolded Lady Justice symbolize?
opts: That justice cannot see or respond to the suffering of those without resources
That the law is applied impartially, blind to all factors except the relevant facts
That judges make rulings based on personal judgment rather than written law
That Canada's justice system operates independently from all government influence
exp: The blindfolded Lady Justice (the Scales of Justice, Vancouver Law Courts) symbolizes the impartial manner in which our laws are administered: blind to all considerations but the facts.

q: What types of courts exist in most provinces in Canada?
opts: Each province has a single superior court that handles all legal matters
An appeal court and a trial court, plus provincial courts handling lesser offences and family matters
Only federally established courts that apply a single system of law across provinces
Each province is required to maintain exactly three levels of court by the Constitution
exp: In most provinces there is an appeal court and a trial court, sometimes called the Court of Queen's Bench or the Supreme Court. There are also provincial courts for lesser offences, family courts, traffic courts and small claims courts for civil cases involving small sums of money.

q: What is the origin of the fleur-de-lys in Canadian history?
opts: Created by French Canadians after 1867 Confederation as a symbol of Quebec identity
The lily flower adopted by French royalty in 496 AD, symbolizing New France and later Quebec
A symbol used by the Acadian peoples before being officially adopted by the province of Quebec
Brought to New France by Samuel de Champlain as a symbol of French royal authority
exp: The lily flower (fleur-de-lys) was adopted by the French king in the year 496. It became the symbol of French royalty for more than 1,000 years, including the colony of New France. Revived at Confederation, the fleur-de-lys was included in the Canadian Red Ensign. In 1948 Quebec adopted its own flag, based on the Cross and the fleur-de-lys.

q: What is the Clarkson Cup?
opts: The trophy awarded annually to the Canadian Football League's championship-winning team
Established in 2005 by Governor General Adrienne Clarkson — the first of Asian origin — for women's hockey
An award presented for outstanding achievement in Canadian arts and cultural performance
The prize given annually to Canada's most accomplished Olympic athlete
exp: The Clarkson Cup, established in 2005 by Adrienne Clarkson, the 26th Governor General (and the first of Asian origin), is awarded for women's hockey.

q: What was the Canadian Red Ensign?
opts: A provincial flag still flown officially by the Government of Ontario
The flag that served as Canada's unofficial national flag for about 100 years before 1965
The original flag of New France, flown over the colony from its founding until 1763
A purely military flag flown by Canadian armed forces only during wartime
exp: The Canadian Red Ensign served as the Canadian flag for about 100 years. It has been carried officially by veterans since 2005.

q: What is the Stanley Cup and who donated it?
opts: The World Hockey Championship trophy donated by the first Prime Minister
The championship trophy for professional hockey, donated by Lord Stanley, the Governor General, in 1892
A trophy for amateur hockey created in 1917 when the NHL was founded
A Canadian Olympic gold medal trophy created in 1920
exp: The National Hockey League plays for the championship Stanley Cup, donated by Lord Stanley, the Governor General, in 1892.

q: What is Sir John A. Macdonald Day?
opts: July 1 — Canada Day, which was proposed and championed by Sir John A. Macdonald
January 11 — recognized by Parliament as Sir John A. Macdonald Day, marking his birthday
November 20 — the date of Sir John A. Macdonald's death in office
October 1 — the anniversary of the date he was first sworn in as Prime Minister
exp: Parliament has recognized January 11 as Sir John A. Macdonald Day — marking his birthday (he was born January 11, 1815).

q: When is Sir Wilfrid Laurier Day?
opts: January 11
July 1
November 20
November 11
exp: November 20 is Sir Wilfrid Laurier Day — one of Canada's national public holidays listed in the study guide.

q: What are the Books of Remembrance?
opts: Historical records of all Acts of Parliament
Books in the Peace Tower's Memorial Chamber listing Canadians who died in military service
Records of all Canadian citizens who received the Order of Canada
Official lists of all Governors General since Confederation
exp: The Memorial Chamber within the Peace Tower contains the Books of Remembrance in which are written the names of soldiers, sailors and airmen who died serving Canada in wars or while on duty.

q: What is Victoria Day and when is it celebrated?
opts: A holiday on May 1 marking Queen Victoria's coronation
The Monday preceding May 25 — celebrating the Sovereign's birthday
A holiday on June 24 celebrating Quebec's patron saint
The second Monday of May celebrating Canadian culture
exp: Victoria Day is celebrated on the Monday preceding May 25 — the Sovereign's birthday. It is a national public holiday.

q: What is the Fête nationale in Quebec and when is it celebrated?
opts: Quebec's provincial holiday on July 1, coinciding with Canada Day
June 24 — the Feast of St. John the Baptist — Quebec's national holiday
The second Monday of June celebrating French-Canadian culture
A Quebec holiday on October 24 marking Confederation
exp: The Fête nationale (Quebec) is celebrated on June 24 — the Feast of St. John the Baptist. It is Quebec's provincial holiday and one of Canada's national public holidays.

q: What does natural resources industry include?
opts: Only oil, natural gas, and petroleum extraction operations
Forestry, fishing, agriculture, mining, and energy — industries vital to Canada's history and economy
Only renewable energy sources such as wind, solar, and hydroelectric power
Manufacturing, technology, and the advanced services sector
exp: Natural resources industries include forestry, fishing, agriculture, mining and energy. These industries have played an important part in the country's history and development. Today, the economy of many areas of the country still depends on developing natural resources.

q: What does manufacturing industry in Canada produce?
opts: Primarily automobiles, steel products, and heavy industrial machinery
Paper, high-tech equipment, aerospace products, automobiles, food, clothing, and other goods
Exclusively raw natural resource commodities processed for international export
Primarily military hardware, defence systems, and government procurement contracts
exp: Manufacturing industries make products to sell in Canada and around the world. Manufactured products include paper, high technology equipment, aerospace technology, automobiles, machinery, food, clothing and many other goods.

q: What does NAFTA stand for and what does it encompass?
opts: North American Federation of Trade Allies — a security and trade pact
North American Free Trade Agreement — covering over 444 million people and trillions in trade
National Agreement for Free Trade with America — a bilateral Canada-US deal
Northern Atlantic Free Trade Area — a multilateral agreement among Atlantic nations
exp: Mexico became a partner in 1994 in the broader North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), with over 444 million people and over $1 trillion in merchandise trade in 2008.

q: What is the Confederation Bridge and what provinces does it connect?
opts: A major bridge connecting mainland New Brunswick to mainland Nova Scotia
One of the longest continuous multispan bridges in the world, connecting PEI to New Brunswick
A bridge connecting Ontario and Quebec across the St. Lawrence River near Montreal
A bridge connecting the British Columbia mainland to Vancouver Island
exp: P.E.I. is connected to mainland Canada by one of the longest continuous multispan bridges in the world, the Confederation Bridge. At almost 13 kilometres in length, the bridge is the longest in the world to cross water that freezes in winter.

q: What is Winnipeg's most famous street intersection and what is St. Boniface?
opts: Main and Broadway — St. Boniface is Winnipeg's arts district
Portage and Main — St. Boniface is Winnipeg's French Quarter with Western Canada's largest Francophone community
King and Queen Streets — St. Boniface is Winnipeg's historic district
Osborne and Corydon — St. Boniface is a suburb of Winnipeg
exp: The province's most populous city is Winnipeg, whose Exchange District includes the most famous street intersection in Canada, Portage and Main. Winnipeg's French Quarter, St. Boniface, has Western Canada's largest Francophone community at 45,000.

q: What percentage of Manitoba's population is of Ukrainian origin and what is notable about its Aboriginal population?
opts: About 5% of Ukrainian origin; Manitoba has the smallest Aboriginal population in Canada
About 14% of Ukrainian origin; Manitoba has the largest Aboriginal population of any province, over 15%
About 20% of Ukrainian origin; Manitoba has the second-largest Aboriginal population in Canada
About 10% of Ukrainian origin; Manitoba's Aboriginal population is equal to Saskatchewan's
exp: Manitoba is also an important centre of Ukrainian culture, with 14% reporting Ukrainian origins, and the largest Aboriginal population of any province, at over 15%.

q: What is Newfoundland and Labrador's distinction geographically?
opts: It is the most northerly province in Canada
It is the most easterly point in North America and has its own time zone
It is the only island province in Canada
It is the province with the longest coastline in Canada
exp: Newfoundland and Labrador is the most easterly point in North America and has its own time zone. In addition to its natural beauty, the province has a unique heritage linked to the sea.

q: What is the Bay of Fundy known for?
opts: Its exceptional whale watching and marine life
The world's highest tides — it is located in Nova Scotia
Being the site of the first French settlement in Canada
The longest undefended border crossing in the Maritimes
exp: Nova Scotia is known for the world's highest tides in the Bay of Fundy.

q: What is the Okanagan Valley in British Columbia known for?
opts: Its salmon fishing and forestry industry
Its fruit orchards and wine industry
Its gold mining and natural resources
Its high-tech industry and innovation centres
exp: B.C. is also known for mining, fishing, and the fruit orchards and wine industry of the Okanagan Valley.

q: What is the most spoken language in BC cities after English?
opts: French — reflecting Canada's status as an officially bilingual country
Chinese and Punjabi — reflecting the province's large and established Asian communities
Cantonese only — the dominant language of BC's oldest immigrant communities
Spanish — reflecting immigration from Latin American countries
exp: The province's large Asian communities have made Chinese and Punjabi the most spoken languages in the cities after English.

q: What is the 'Land of the Midnight Sun'?
opts: A nickname for the northern regions of British Columbia and the Yukon Territory
The North — where summer daylight can last up to 24 hours and winter brings months of darkness
A name used exclusively for the territory of Nunavut in federal government documents
A term historically used only for the Yukon during the Klondike Gold Rush era
exp: The North is often referred to as the 'Land of the Midnight Sun' because at the height of summer, daylight can last up to 24 hours. In winter, the sun disappears and darkness sets in for three months.

q: What is the Mackenzie River and what is its significance?
opts: The longest river in Canada, flowing through British Columbia to the Pacific
At 4,200 km, one of North America's longest river systems, flowing through the Northwest Territories
A major river that forms part of the international boundary between Canada and the USA
The primary water source supplying irrigation for the Prairie Provinces
exp: The Mackenzie River, at 4,200 kilometres, is the second-longest river system in North America after the Mississippi and drains an area of 1.8 million square kilometres. It flows through the Northwest Territories.

q: What is Yellowknife known as and why?
opts: 'The Oil Capital of the North' — due to massive oil reserves
'The diamond capital of North America' — capital of the Northwest Territories with about 20,000 people
'The Gold Capital of Canada' — due to historic gold mining
'The Gateway to the Arctic' — due to its northern location
exp: The capital of the Northwest Territories, Yellowknife (population 20,000), is called the 'diamond capital of North America.'

q: What is the coldest temperature ever recorded in Canada and where?
opts: -50°C in Nunavut
-63°C in the Yukon
-55°C in the Northwest Territories
-45°C in northern Manitoba
exp: Yukon holds the record for the coldest temperature ever recorded in Canada (-63°C).

q: What is Mount Logan and who is it named after?
opts: Canada's highest mountain, located in Alberta and named after a fur trade explorer
Canada's highest peak, in the Yukon, named for Sir William Logan, a celebrated geologist
Canada's highest mountain, in the Rockies of Alberta, named after a Prime Minister
A major peak in the Northwest Territories named after a famous Arctic expedition leader
exp: Mount Logan, located in the Yukon, is the highest mountain in Canada. It is named in honour of Sir William Logan, a world-famous geologist, born in Montreal in 1798 to Scottish immigrant parents. Logan founded and directed the Geological Survey of Canada from 1842 to 1869 and is considered one of Canada's greatest scientists.

q: What does the tundra in the North consist of?
opts: Dense boreal forests and frozen lakes covering thousands of square kilometres
A vast, treeless Arctic plain with permanently frozen soil, where some hunt, fish, and trap
Open grasslands similar in character and climate to the southern Prairie Provinces
Coastal wetlands, salt marshes, and swamps formed by tidal activity
exp: Much of the North is made up of tundra, the vast rocky Arctic plain. Because of the cold Arctic climate, there are no trees on the tundra and the soil is permanently frozen. Some continue to earn a living by hunting, fishing and trapping. Inuit art is sold throughout Canada and around the world.

q: What is the Canadian Rangers?
opts: A federal law enforcement agency based in Canada's three northern territories
Part-time Canadian Forces Reserves who address security and sovereignty in the North using Indigenous knowledge
A volunteer organization that fights wildfires in remote northern Canadian communities
A dedicated search and rescue organization operating exclusively within the Arctic Circle
exp: Canada's vast North brings security and sovereignty challenges. The Canadian Rangers, part of the Canadian Forces Reserves (militia), play a key role. Drawing on Indigenous knowledge and experience, the Rangers travel by snowmobile in the winter and all-terrain vehicles in the summer from Resolute to the Magnetic North Pole, and keep the flag flying in Canada's Arctic.

q: What is Quebec's role in pulp and paper production?
opts: Quebec is the smallest producer of pulp and paper in Canada
Quebec is Canada's main producer of pulp and paper
Quebec exports pulp and paper only to France
Quebec's pulp and paper industry was shut down in the 1990s
exp: Quebec is Canada's main producer of pulp and paper.

q: What makes Ontario unique in terms of French-speaking population?
opts: Ontario has no significant French-speaking population outside of Ottawa
Ontario has the largest French-speaking population outside Quebec, with a strong heritage of language preservation
Ontario is officially bilingual, like New Brunswick, under the federal Official Languages Act
Ontario has a larger French-speaking population than New Brunswick in absolute numbers
exp: Founded by United Empire Loyalists, Ontario also has the largest French-speaking population outside of Quebec, with a proud history of preserving their language and culture.

q: What is the Niagara region in Ontario known for?
opts: Its automobile manufacturing plants
Its vineyards, wines and fruit crops
Its steel production and heavy industry
Its technology and innovation sector
exp: The Niagara region is known for its vineyards, wines and fruit crops.

q: What is the 19-member Legislative Assembly of Nunavut and how does it choose its leaders?
opts: Elected by political party affiliation, with the winning party forming the territorial government
The 19-member Assembly chooses a premier and ministers by consensus, with no political parties
Appointed directly by the federal government in Ottawa on the Prime Minister's recommendation
Elected every three years in territory-wide votes open to all residents over the age of 16
exp: The 19-member Legislative Assembly chooses a premier and ministers by consensus. The population is about 85% Inuit, and Inuktitut is an official language and the first language in schools.
